# @heretek-ai/opencode-teamwork-v2

An **OpenCode V2 port** of [`opencode-teamwork`](https://github.com/aditya0si/OpenCode-Team) —
Antigravity-style multi-agent orchestration for OpenCode.

The original package only implements the **OpenCode V1 plugin API**, so it fails
to load on OpenCode V2:

```
failed to load plugin
PluginModule.LoadError: Plugin must export a default definition with an id and
an effect or setup function. (cause: SchemaError(Expected object at ["default"]))
```

This repo is the ported, V2-native version: the original 10 agents plus a
security auditor, document segment reviewer, formalization reviewer,
tournament referee, and independent victory auditor (15 total) and 7 slash commands,
rewritten for the V2 plugin + agent APIs. Verified against **OpenCode 2.4.1**.
`package.json` declares an **optional** peer range `@opencode/plugin: ^2.4` (optional so
the package stays dependency-free), and `setup` warns when `ctx.app.version` is outside
the verified 2.4 pair.

## What changed (V1 → V2)

| Original (V1) | This port (V2) |
| --- | --- |
| Default export = async plugin function returning a `config` hook | Default export = `{ id, setup }` definition (exactly what `Plugin.define({...})` returns) |
| `config` hook injects 10 agents | **Not possible in a V2 plugin** — the `AgentEditor` has no `add`. Agents are installed as markdown files: `agents/team/*.md` |
| `config` hook injects 7 commands | Registered by the plugin via `ctx.command.transform(...)` → `editor.add(...)` |
| Commands used `{{ ... }}` handlebars + `agent:` frontmatter | V2 has neither; `$ARGUMENTS` substitution in the plugin, agent switching via `ctx.session.switchAgent(...)` |
| Agent perms `edit/bash/webfetch/task` | V2 `permissions` array: `edit/shell/webfetch/subagent` |

## Layout

```
package.json                      # npm manifest (name: @heretek-ai/opencode-teamwork-v2)
index → plugins/opencode-teamwork/index.ts   # V2 plugin, registers the 7 commands
plugins/opencode-teamwork/tools.ts           # engine tools + hooks (V2 API)
plugins/opencode-teamwork/document-review.ts # Document Review route classifier, PDF/MD ingestion, RSA bounds
plugins/opencode-teamwork/lemma.ts           # LEMMA (Lean 4) probe, classifier, verifier
plugins/opencode-teamwork/tournament.ts      # bounded massive-proof tournament & opt-in router
plugins/opencode-teamwork/safe-fs.mjs        # shared bounded read + pinned/detective write containment (ADR 0004/0010/0013)
agents/team/*.md                  # 15 team agents (markdown, V2 frontmatter)
docs/ARTIFACTS.md                 # canonical artifact layout, topologies, schemas
lib/team.mjs                      # installer core (config dir, model map, agent files)
lib/picker.mjs                    # interactive model picker (`opencode models`)
lib/runs.mjs                      # run inspection, DAG visualization, worktree pruning
lib/doctor.mjs                    # environment diagnostic health checks
lib/timeline.mjs                  # chronological run lifecycle builder & renderer
lib/export.mjs                    # read-only run report builder (HTML / Markdown export)
lib/approve.mjs                   # authenticated prompt-approval producer/verifier (`approve …`)
bin/opencode-teamwork.mjs         # CLI: init / models / install / status / doctor / runs / inspect / timeline / export / prune / approve
scripts/lint-prompts.mjs          # prompt linter (run in CI)
scripts/test-cost.mjs             # session tree consumption tests
scripts/test-engine.mjs           # DAG engine, security gate & worktree tests
scripts/test-approval.mjs         # authenticated prompt-approval parity (print + TUI)
scripts/test-doctor.mjs           # hermetic environment & CLI doctor tests
scripts/test-timeline.mjs         # timeline hermetic unit tests
postinstall.mjs                   # asks for models during npm install
```

## Engine (tools + hooks)

The run mechanics are real, not prompt prose. The plugin registers deterministic
tools and runtime permission hooks. Each registration carries
`options: { namespace: "teamwork", codemode: false }`: OpenCode's effective id is
`namespace + "_" + name` (`packages/core/src/tool/runtime.ts`), so the model sees
direct `teamwork_*` tools (the same ids the agents and command templates call)
rather than Code Mode-only `teamwork.plan` entries. The table below lists the
exposed ids:

| Tool | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `teamwork_budget` | budget preflight: console credit derivation |
| `teamwork_route` | priority-ordered route classifier (`document-review` first and before Math/Proof, then explicit Lean 4/LEMMA, then opt-in `massive-proof`; rejects PR/code reviews, bare filenames without a supplied doc, and theorem-solving requests) |
| `teamwork_plan` | create the run dir + signed `run.manifest.json` / `plan.dag.json` / `state.json` / `costs.json` (with pre-`mkdir` tournament preflight) |
| `teamwork_document_triage` | ingest/partition a supplied document into `seg-01`..`seg-0K` + `doc-synthesis` with pre-`mkdir` bounds & path containment checks; live URLs go through the SSRF guard |
| `teamwork_document_record` | persist bounded RSA tree node outputs, `unit-report.md`, `candidate-<I>.md`, and `DOCUMENT_REVIEW_REPORT.md` |
| `teamwork_tournament` | bounded `massive-proof` tournament state machine (`estimate`, `init`, `propose`, `falsify`, `merge`, `score`, `audit`, `cancel`, `status`) |
| `teamwork_preflight` | re-check a run's named inputs, write `preflight.json` (reports, never blocks) |
| `teamwork_status` | per-task progress for the active run |
| `teamwork_resume` | tasks still open, for a restart |
| `teamwork_cost` | read real spend across the OpenCode session tree (sentinel + workers + verifiers) against the **advisory** run budget (warns at 80%; only massive-proof tournaments enforce the threshold); snapshot updates are digest-idempotent |
| `teamwork_pitfall` | append to the pitfall registry (dynamically injected into workers) |
| `teamwork_next` | evaluates DAG dependencies, lifecycle states, and ready tasks; atomically leases each ready task (5 min + 5 min grace on claim protocol 2) with a monotonic fence so concurrent resumes cannot dispatch duplicates; a stale claim is reclaimed only when the side-effect fingerprint is unchanged, otherwise `needs-inspection`; strict runs stop at `NEEDS_STRICT_WAVE` until both wave verdicts exist |
| `teamwork_task_update` | deterministic task state machine transitions (`pending` → `worker_active` → `worker_done` → `verifier_active` → `verified_pass` / `verified_fail` / `blocked`); every protocol-2 transition enforces the claim fence/ownership (`STALE_FENCE`, `CLAIM_OWNED_BY_OTHER`, `CLAIM_EXPIRED`), a reasoned Sentinel override is recorded, and terminal states release the claim |
| `teamwork_recover` | explicit crash recovery for a claim: `heartbeat`, `inspect` (single-use hashed 10-minute token), `release`, `block`, `requeue`, `adopt` (clean committed branch → `worker_done`, no new commit), `discard` (force+confirm); never auto-commits |
| `teamwork_handoff` | trusted five-section handoff writer (`handoffs/<taskId\|_run>-<role>.md` + bounded `handoffs/index.json`); continuity evidence required by `final_verify`/`next` when `requireHandoffs: "required"`, never a gate verdict |
| `teamwork_report` | trusted writer for a signed `verify/report-<taskId>.json`: caller must be `team/verifier`, descend from the run root, and name an existing task; a `PASS` needs a summary or check |
| `teamwork_security_audit` | mandatory pre-merge security gate (`verify/security-audit.json`; signed on a signed run) |
| `teamwork_victory_audit` | record the independent `team/victory-auditor` acceptance verdict, bound to the current `ORIGINAL_REQUEST.md` and `requirements.json` hashes (`verify/victory.json`); caller must descend from the run root |
| `teamwork_evidence` | write one bounded evidence artifact under `verify/evidence/<name>` (64 KiB, 32 files) through the pinned run writer; returns `{path, sha256, bytes}` so `teamwork_wave_record` can cite it. Bytes, not a verdict |
| `teamwork_wave_record` | strict mode only: record one `team/falsifier` challenge (`PASS`) or `team/security-auditor` audit (`CLEAN`) per task (`verify/challenge-<task>.json` / `verify/audit-<task>.json`); trusted caller identity + session tree, sha256-bound to the verifier report (same-report write-once, changed-report replace) |
| `teamwork_final_verify` | compute the final verdict from the task reports + security audit + victory audit (plus the strict wave when enabled, and `lemma/` artifacts when in LEMMA mode), verify the signed baseline, stamp it, write signed `verify/final.json` |
| `teamwork_lemma_probe` | read-only probe for `lean`, `lake`, and the LEAP CLI (`leap`; legacy `leap-tools` accepted) on `PATH` |
| `teamwork_lemma_formalize` | LEMMA Phase 0 `problem_draft.lean` / `review_pre` → `problem.lean` and `review_final` faithfulness gate |
| `teamwork_lemma_node` | bounded lemma decomposition tree (`create`, `update`, `blueprint`, `attempt`) |
| `teamwork_lemma_verify` | execute real `lean`/`lake` verification with `sorry`/admit/axiom rejection, stamping `verify-<r>.json` |
| `teamwork_worktree` | out-of-repo git worktree provisioning, diff, merge, resolve & cleanup; `setup` records the claim baseline and renews it, `diff` returns HEAD/baseSha/diffHash, `merge` refuses `BRANCH_MOVED`, `cleanup` refuses a live claim, and a foreign run host refuses destructive actions unless explicitly allowed |

**Tool authorization.** Plugin tools are not mediated by the permission hook,
so every run-mutating `teamwork_*` tool checks the caller itself
(`authorize.ts`). The trusted session agent (`ctx.session.get`) must match the
tool/action lane and, for run-bound tools, the caller must descend from the
plan-time `rootSessionId`; a caller-supplied `agent` label is never authority.
Examples: `teamwork_plan`/`teamwork_document_triage` are sentinel/crafter lanes,
`teamwork_security_audit` is `team/security-auditor` only,
`teamwork_final_verify` is `team/verifier`/sentinel, `teamwork_lemma_node` is
`team/proof-worker`, and tournament `propose`/`falsify`/`merge`/`score` are
`proposer`/`falsifier`/`synthesizer`/`referee` respectively. Unresolved identity
fails closed for mutating tools. Read-only `teamwork_status`,
`teamwork_resume`, and `teamwork_cost` stay available to every installed
`team/*` role. See `docs/GUARDRAILS.md` for the full matrix.

**URL network policy.** `document.url` ingestion and preflight URL checks use
`url-guard.ts`: http/https only, public addresses only (loopback, private,
link-local, metadata, multicast, reserved, and IPv4-mapped IPv6 are rejected),
DNS answers are validated and the connection is pinned to them, redirects are
not followed (a `Location` is validated before refusal), and timeouts/size caps
apply. `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_ALLOW_LOCALHOST=1` is the explicit test/development
opt-in that permits loopback only; the default is deny.

Hooks: `permission.evaluate` enforces the per-agent read-only policy **in code**
(not just in their prompts). The read-only agents (`team/verifier`,
`team/falsifier`, `team/scout`, `team/security-auditor`,
`team/segment-reviewer`, `team/formalization-reviewer`, `team/referee`,
`team/victory-auditor`) all deny the `edit` tool, so none of them can write
through it. `shell` is still available to the verifier, scout, security auditor
and victory auditor, and it can modify files; the falsifier, segment reviewer,
formalization reviewer, and referee also have `shell` denied, and the segment,
formalization, referee, and victory-auditor roles deny `webfetch` and
`subagent` as well (the verifier and security auditor deny `webfetch`). In
short: no writes through `edit` for all eight, and no `shell` writes for the
falsifier, segment reviewer, formalization reviewer, or referee. The
`team/victory-auditor` keeps `shell` (it can modify files) and is denied `edit`,
`webfetch`, and `subagent`; its independence comes from a fresh session that
inspects the delivered artifacts and runs tests itself, not from capability
isolation.
The hook also enforces network constraints: when the active run's
`constraints.network` is `denied` (read from `prompt_draft.md` or a per-task
`spec.json`), `webfetch` is denied for **every** `team/*` agent — sentinel,
workers, verifiers, reviewers and auditors alike. `shell` network access is
still honor-system: the permission layer cannot sandbox it. `session.context`
injects the active run's state + recent pitfalls into every team agent's system
prompt.

All run artifacts live under `.opencode/teamwork/<session-id>/`; see
[`docs/ARTIFACTS.md`](docs/ARTIFACTS.md) for the layout, the canonical
topologies, and the JSON schemas (`spec.json`, `plan.dag.json`, `state.json`,
`verification_report.json`). The installer copies that reference to
`<config-dir>/teamwork/ARTIFACTS.md` next to your agents.

### Completion guarantees

- `verified_pass` requires a legal lifecycle transition and PASS evidence (an inline PASS verdict or a `PASS` per-task report).
- A plan writes a signed `run.manifest.json` (the default). Verifier reports, security audit, strict-wave verdicts, victory verdict, and final verdict carry an `_auth` envelope and a `ctx.storage` digest-index entry. `final_verify`/`next` fail as `AUTH_MISSING`, `AUTH_INVALID`, `AUTH_UNKNOWN_KEY`, `AUTH_INDEX_MISSING`, or `AUTH_STALE` when an artifact is forged, copied, edited, or the signed plan/requirements/policy baseline drifts. See [`docs/adr/0005-artifact-authenticity.md`](docs/adr/0005-artifact-authenticity.md).
- `_auth` supports HMAC-SHA256 (backward-compatible `mac`) and Ed25519 (`sig`). Every new signed run pins a 128-bit `runNonce` and `runKeyId` in the manifest, so a cross-run copy or a rotated re-sign fails. With Ed25519, verification needs only the SPKI public key. `teamwork_plan` also records `trustLevel` (`local-hmac` default, `external-signer`, `human-approved`, `ci-attested`) and optional `requireWitness`; `final_verify` enforces the level, and `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER`/`OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_WITNESS` fail closed (`AUTH_SIGNER_UNAVAILABLE`/`AUTH_WITNESS_UNAVAILABLE`). 0.14.0 signs witness receipts (`OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_WITNESS_PUBLIC_KEY`) so a forged KV record is `AUTH_INVALID`, labels a receipt `unverified` without that key, and adds signer protocol v2 plus `opencode-teamwork approve signer` when `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER_APPROVAL_DIR` is set. `human-approved`/`ci-attested` require an Ed25519 approval from `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_APPROVAL_DIR`, signed by a key distinct from the run key and bound to the **exact bytes of `prompt_draft.md`** plus the run id and a one-use nonce (0.11.0; manifest version 3). The plan verifies it before any `mkdir`, `final_verify` re-hashes the draft, and a re-plan cannot change the binding. The plugin/command signer refuses `approvals/` paths (`AUTH_APPROVAL_SCOPE`). See [`docs/adr/0011-authenticated-prompt-approval.md`](docs/adr/0011-authenticated-prompt-approval.md), [`docs/adr/0008-signer-spi-and-trust-levels.md`](docs/adr/0008-signer-spi-and-trust-levels.md) and [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md).
- A run completes only with a `PASS` `verify/final.json` stamped by `teamwork_final_verify`; an unstamped report needs the recorded `allowUnstamped` bypass. An unsigned legacy run returns `AUTH_LEGACY` until the recorded `allowUnsignedLegacy` bypass is passed at the completion gate; `benchmark` refuses that bypass, `victoryAudit: "skip"`, and `requireHandoffs: "skip"`.

## First run (5 minutes)

1. Install the plugin: `opencode plugin add @heretek-ai/opencode-teamwork-v2`.

2. Assign models and install the agents. `init` writes
   `~/.config/opencode/teamwork.json`, installs all 15 agents and registers the
   plugin; `models` rewrites only the model map and the agents' `model:` lines.
   Both are safe to re-run.

   ```sh
   npx @heretek-ai/opencode-teamwork-v2 init
   npx @heretek-ai/opencode-teamwork-v2 models
   ```

3. In your project, run `/teamwork-craft`. The 9-step interview writes the
   approved spec to `.opencode/teamwork/<session-id>/prompt_draft.md`.

4. Review it, then run `/teamwork <session-id>`. Planning enforces the **spec
   presence gate**: a non-empty `prompt_draft.md` must exist. The explicit
   bypass is `skipInterview: true` on `teamwork_plan`, recorded as
   `specGate: "bypassed"`. Presence is not proof of user approval:
   `skipInterview` / `requireSpec: false` are caller-controlled and recorded,
   not an approval signature.

   For `trustLevel: "human-approved"` / `"ci-attested"`, produce an
   authenticated approval **before** the plan, from a process that holds the
   approver key and writes outside the repo/run:

   ```sh
   # inspect what will be signed (writes nothing trusted)
   opencode-teamwork approve request --session <session-id> --approver uid:alice

   # sign the exact draft bytes with the Ed25519 approver key
   opencode-teamwork approve sign --request request.json \
     --draft .opencode/teamwork/<session-id>/prompt_draft.md \
     --key ~/.config/opencode/approver.pem --approver uid:alice --ttl 24h

   # re-run the plan-time checks at any time
   opencode-teamwork approve verify --session <session-id>
   ```

   `approve sign` refuses a draft that still contains `[OPEN:` unless
   `--allow-open` records the gaps (the plan then refuses that approval), and
   asks the operator to retype the first 8 hex characters of the draft digest
   and the word `approve`. The approval binds the draft, the run id, and a
   one-use nonce; it does **not** prove a human read the draft (see
   [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md)).

5. The run directory `.opencode/teamwork/<session-id>/` holds `plan.dag.json`
   (the task DAG), per-task `verify/report-<task>.json` reports, and
   `verify/final.json` — written and stamped by `teamwork_final_verify`, never
   by hand.

6. Inspect it afterwards from the project root:

   ```sh
   npx @heretek-ai/opencode-teamwork-v2 status     # install + model map
   npx @heretek-ai/opencode-teamwork-v2 timeline   # per-task timing, rounds, spend
   npx @heretek-ai/opencode-teamwork-v2 export     # HTML report (-m for Markdown)
   ```

### LEMMA (Lean 4 formal-proof route)

LEMMA is an explicit opt-in capability-gated route (`topology: "proof"`, `lemmaMode: true`) for Lean 4 proving and verification:

- **Explicit opt-in only:** `teamwork_route` checks `document-review` first, requires an explicit Lean 4 prove/formalize/verify/check request in prose, ignores instructions inside fenced code blocks, and routes unrequested `.lean` or Lean-syntax tasks to `distributed-coding` (never `proof`).
- **Pre-spending toolchain gate:** Requires user-installed **Lean 4** (`lean` and `lake` via `elan`) and the **LEAP CLI** (`leap`) on `PATH`; the legacy `leap-tools` name is also accepted. If any is missing, `teamwork_plan` refuses **before `mkdir`** (zero run files created, zero budget spent) and prints install instructions for both.
  - Install the pinned CLI with `pipx install git+https://github.com/billkunghappy/LEAP-CLI@afc016d23579d8236050a157fe6cac8f17b13096` (the `leap-tools` PyPI package does not exist). `leap lean` is the optional full Mathlib setup (~11 GB, 10–20 minutes); LEMMA verification needs only core Lean, no Mathlib.
- **Bounded verification:** Phase 0 formalization (`problem_draft.lean` → `team/formalization-reviewer` `APPROVE` → `problem.lean`), bounded lemma tree (`maxDepth <= 3`, `maxWidth <= 4`, `maxNodes <= 24`, `maxRetries <= 4`), real `lean`/`lake` execution via `teamwork_lemma_verify` rejecting `sorry`/`admit`/unauthorized `axiom` even on exit `0`, and final `FAITHFUL` check before `teamwork_final_verify`.
- **Declaration and axiom binding:** each node records its Lean `declaration` and `statement`. Before a node becomes `proved`/`disproved`, the attempt must declare that name and type (comments, strings, and syntax quotations are masked; duplicate/namespaced/`private`/`protected` declarations fail closed). The verifier then runs `#print axioms <declaration>` and records `declaration`, `declarationType`, `axiomDependencies`, and `unauthorizedAxioms`, accepting only `Classical.choice`, `propext`, `Quot.sound`, plus axioms approved once at plan time via `lemmaPolicy.allowedAxioms` (persisted in `lemma/manifest.json`). `sorryAx` is always rejected, and `#`/`logInfo`/`dbg_trace`/`trace`/`run_cmd`/`println`/`IO.`/`set_option trace` probe-hijacking attempts fail closed. Node statement/declaration metadata is immutable after a PASS; `teamwork_final_verify` re-checks stamped metadata before accepting a run.
- **Known limits:** binding compares the elaborated type text lexically (binder/negation spellings normalized), not semantic equality; the transitive-axiom allowlist is approved at plan time (`lemmaPolicy.allowedAxioms`) and persisted in `lemma/manifest.json`, never caller-supplied at verify time; and the live Lean path is not exercised on hosts without `lean`/`lake`/`leap` (the E2E test skips loudly, while stub tests cover the control flow). CI installs core Lean + the LEAP CLI (no Mathlib) so the live E2E runs on every relevant pull request.

## High-assurance deployment

The default package is tamper-evident against a writer limited to the run
directory; it is not a boundary against a shell running as the same UID as
OpenCode. If you need a real privilege boundary, the administrator-only path is
documented separately:

- [`docs/ADMIN-HARDENING.md`](docs/ADMIN-HARDENING.md) — a Linux runbook for a
  separate signer UID, a `0700` key directory, a root-owned signer, a systemd
  socket service, audit rules and SELinux labels. Every step has a proof, a
  rollback and an honest limit.
- [`docs/SIGNER-PROTOCOL.md`](docs/SIGNER-PROTOCOL.md) — the v2 signer contract
  that turns a command signer from an oracle into a policy-enforcing signer.
  0.14.0 sends v2 (with `runId` and a derived `approvalRef`) when
  `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER_APPROVAL_DIR` is set, and the exact v1 request
  otherwise. The signer itself is not shipped: it must be built and installed,
  and a version mismatch fails closed with `AUTH_SIGNER_UNAVAILABLE`.
- [`scripts/hardening-check.sh`](scripts/hardening-check.sh) — a read-only
  Linux verifier that prints `PASS`/`FAIL`/`UNKNOWN` per probe. It never
  modifies the host; `UNKNOWN` is not a pass.

These are deployment changes, not plugin features. They do not make the plugin,
the prompts or the model trustworthy, and none of the steps is executed
automatically. `opencode-teamwork doctor --security --require-hardened` remains
the plugin-side posture check.

## Notes

- The plugin is intentionally **dependency-free at runtime** — it does not import
  `@opencode/plugin`, so the loader never needs to resolve `node_modules` for it.
  The exported object shape is identical to `Plugin.define({ id, setup })`.
- V2 agents cannot be created by a plugin, so the plugin only registers commands,
  ships the `teamwork_*` engine tools, and verifies (never writes) the `team/*.md`

  prefer no plugin at all, move the 7 command definitions into markdown files

  no blocking `effect: ask` in parallel agents) are enforced by
  `scripts/lint-prompts.mjs` — run `npm run lint:prompts`. CI runs it whenever

- **Security:** the guardrail model (path containment, server-derived session
  ids, read-only enforcement, signed control-plane artifacts, sanitised context
  injection, non-destructive installers) is documented in
  [`docs/GUARDRAILS.md`](docs/GUARDRAILS.md) and
  [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md). Artifact authenticity is tamper-evident against
  a run-dir-only writer, but **a same-UID shell with read access to
  `opencode.db` / the plugin KV store can read a local HMAC or Ed25519 private

  [`docs/adr/0006-artifact-trust-isolation.md`](docs/adr/0006-artifact-trust-isolation.md);

  The `team/security-auditor` agent audits a repo with a clean context.

> **Artifact-trust boundary (ADR 0005/0006/0008):** signed control-plane
> artifacts are tamper-evident against a writer limited to the run directory.

# Security model and artifact-trust boundary

This document states what `@heretek-ai/opencode-teamwork-v2` does and does not
protect, and how to choose a trust level. The implementation decisions are in
[ADR 0005](docs/adr/0005-artifact-authenticity.md),
[ADR 0006](docs/adr/0006-artifact-trust-isolation.md) and
[ADR 0008](docs/adr/0008-signer-spi-and-trust-levels.md). Handoff provenance is
a sibling extension of ADR 0005, specified in
[ADR 0007](docs/adr/0007-signed-handoff-provenance.md). Evidence binding and
contradiction detection are specified in
[ADR 0012](docs/adr/0012-evidence-binding-and-contradiction-detection.md).
Verifiable witness receipts and signer protocol v2 are specified in
[ADR 0014](docs/adr/0014-verifiable-witness-and-signer-v2.md). Offline
verification from bytes and a public key is specified in
[ADR 0015](docs/adr/0015-offline-verification.md). Re-execution of recorded
command evidence is specified in
[ADR 0016](docs/adr/0016-re-executable-verification.md).

## What is protected

Control-plane artifacts — `run.manifest.json`, `verify/report-<task>.json`,
`verify/security-audit.json`, `verify/challenge-<task>.json`,
`verify/audit-<task>.json`, `verify/victory.json`, and `verify/final.json` —
carry an `_auth` envelope over their exact run-relative path plus a canonical
JSON digest. Every signed run pins a 128-bit `runNonce` and a `runKeyId` in the
signed manifest, and each artifact also has a digest-index entry outside the run
directory (`auth/run/<runId>/<relPath>` in `ctx.storage`).

Against a writer limited to the run directory, the envelope and index make these
attacks detectable:

- forging a verifier report, security audit, strict-wave verdict, victory
  verdict, or final verdict;
- flipping a signed verdict field after the write;
- copying an `_auth` envelope between files or between runs (path, nonce, key
  id, and index all bind the artifact to one run);
- re-signing a rotated run with a different key id (the manifest's `runKeyId` is
  pinned);
- downgrading `verification`, `victoryAudit`, `requireHandoffs`,
  `integrityMode`, the plan, the request, the requirements baseline, or the
  LEMMA axiom policy after the plan.

With an Ed25519 key, **verification needs only the SPKI public key**. A verifier
does not need the private key, and does not need to trust the signer's claimed
algorithm or key id: the envelope algorithm is fixed to `ed25519`, the key id is
pinned by the manifest, and the signature is checked against the configured
public key before the artifact is accepted.

### Evidence binding: bytes, facts, observation

0.12.0 makes each verdict name the evidence it reviewed and the gate recompute
that relation from disk ([ADR 0012](docs/adr/0012-evidence-binding-and-contradiction-detection.md)):

- **Bytes.** A victory binds `evidenceDigests {reports, securityAudit, final}`;
  a verifier report binds the worker handoff body (`workerHandoff`); a security
  audit binds its `reviewedDigests` and its `ruleChecks`; a wave binds cited
  `verify/` files; `verify/evidence/<name>` artifacts are bounded (64 KiB, 32
  per run) and re-hashed. Editing, deleting, resizing, or swapping any of those
  makes the dependent verdict `AUTH_STALE`/`STALE`.
- **Facts.** The engine derives the relations from `plan.dag.json`,
  `handoffs/index.json`, and the files themselves — coverage of every rule
  forbidden at the run's integrity mode, the verifier → worker → report chain,
  and four cross-artifact contradictions
  (`INCONSISTENT_VICTORY_TASK`, `INCONSISTENT_REPORT_BRANCH`,
  `INCONSISTENT_AUDIT_HIGH`, `INCONSISTENT_WAVE_REPORT`). These can make a run
  fail; they cannot make a dishonest claim true.
- **Observation.** The reviewer's judgment (a requirement is met, a rule is
  clean) is recorded, not proven. The engine never parses prose as PASS/FAIL.

> a same-UID writer can still author false content; the engine guarantees the
> false claim is specific, signed, path-bound and digest-chained, so a
> privileged verifier can falsify it.

That sentence is the whole claim. Binding makes a lie **specific and
falsifiable**; it does not detect a false statement at creation, prove that a
reviewer read the artifact, or replace re-execution.

## What is not protected

- **A same-UID process.** A shell running as the OpenCode user can read
  `opencode.db` / the plugin KV store, the local Ed25519 private key, the HMAC
  key, and the digest index. It can mint an envelope and rewrite the index. A
  local `command:` signer that accepts any request from that UID is a signing
  oracle, not a boundary. This is why the package does not describe artifacts
  as tamper-proof or as signed by a trusted authority.
- **A modified plugin or config.** The plugin, agent prompts, and
  `opencode.json` are user-owned; a same-UID writer can disable the gate.
- **A prompt-injected agent with shell access.** The gate authenticates the
  artifact, not the judgment of the agent that wrote it.
- **Root, a malicious kernel/OpenCode binary, a compromised model provider, or
  physical access.**
- **Availability.** A same-UID writer can delete or truncate a run.
- **Secrecy of run artifacts.** Authenticity is not confidentiality.

`opencode-teamwork doctor --security` prints the relevant host facts (key
source/algorithm, signer/witness config, `ptrace_scope`, root-equivalent group
membership, DB mode including `-wal`/`-shm`, config/plugin writability, whether
an approver key is configured and whether its private material is visible to
this UID, whether a configured signer could accept an `approvals/` path, the
prompt-approval directory and its owner, the signer-approval directory and its
owner, write-containment mode, SELinux). A knowable problem is a
`fail`; an uninspectable fact is `unknown`, never "safe".
`doctor --security --require-hardened` exits 2 when any check is `fail` or
`unknown`; plain `doctor --security` is advisory (exit 0 with a warning
summary). The doctor does not turn a warning into protection.

### Write containment is preventive on Linux, detective elsewhere

Run-artifact writers are **preventive** only on Linux with a usable
`/proc/self/fd`: the destination parent is pinned once and every create, mkdir,
rename, write, lstat and unlink is relative to that descriptor (ADR 0010).
**Linux without procfs fails closed**; nothing is written. **macOS and Windows
are detective**: there is no pure-JS dir-relative write without a native addon,
so the writer keeps the path-based atomic write and checks. 0.13.0 records the
run root and every existing ancestor `(dev, ino)` at target time, re-stats them
before the create/rename/unlink and in the post-check, refuses a mismatch as
`identity-changed`, and records the run-root identity in the signed
`run.manifest.json` for a re-check before control-plane writes. A detected swap
is a report about an event that already happened, not a prevented one: bytes may
already be outside the run and are not rolled back, and a transient swap that is
reverted before the check can be missed. A legitimately renamed run root fails
closed.

`OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_REQUIRE_PINNED_WRITES=1` (or a plan's
`requirePinnedWrites: true`) makes the policy explicit: on a host whose mode is
not `pinned`, **control-plane writes are refused** with a named
`containment-mode` refusal. It is off by default. `doctor --security` reports
the mode and the env setting; an asserted policy on a non-pinned host is a
failure, so `--require-hardened` exits 2.

## Trust levels

`teamwork_plan` accepts `trustLevel` (default `local-hmac`). The level is
persisted in `plan.dag.json`, `state.json`, and the signed
`run.manifest.json`; a re-plan may repeat it but never change it. `final_verify`
enforces it.

| Level | Signing | What `final_verify` requires |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `local-hmac` | HMAC-SHA256 key ring in plugin storage (or `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_HMAC_KEY`) | A verified HMAC envelope and index entry. |
| `external-signer` | Local Ed25519 key or `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER=command:<path>` | Verified **Ed25519** envelopes only; an HMAC envelope fails `AUTH_TRUST_LEVEL`. |
| `human-approved` | Any configured run source | An Ed25519 approval in `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_APPROVAL_DIR` bound to the exact `prompt_draft.md` bytes, the run id, and a one-use nonce, with `approvedBy` and a fresh bounded lifetime. |
| `ci-attested` | Any configured run source | The same prompt-bound approval with `attestedBy` and `trustLevel: "ci-attested"`. |

### What `human-approved` / `ci-attested` establish

An approval is a separate Ed25519 `_auth` envelope over
`{runId, trustLevel, binding: "prompt", promptDraftSha256, promptDraftBytes,
openGaps, approvalNonce, approvedAt, expiresAt, planHash?, approvedBy|attestedBy}`.
Since 0.11.0 it binds the **prompt draft**, not only the manifest. The
manifest (version 3) records `specHash`, `specBytes`, `approvalDigest`,
`approvalNonce`, `approvalBinding`, `approvedBy`, and `approvedAt`; a re-plan
that changes any of them is `AUTH_STALE`.

- It must be read from an **absolute approval directory** outside the run and
  the repository, a real directory (never a symlink), owned by a **different
  UID** than the run process. A file must be a regular file, not a symlink, also
  owned by that other UID. A same-UID directory fails
  `AUTH_APPROVAL_UNTRUSTED`; the sandbox cannot satisfy this on one UID.
- Its envelope must be **Ed25519**, and its `_auth.keyId` must be **different**
  from the manifest's `runKeyId`. An HMAC approval or an approval signed with
  the run key fails `AUTH_APPROVAL_NOT_HUMAN`. Configure the verify-only
  approver key with `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_APPROVAL_PUBLIC_KEY` (and optionally
  `_KEY_ID`); the key id is pinned in the signed manifest as `approvalKeyId`.
- It must bind the exact `prompt_draft.md` bytes
  (`promptDraftSha256 === specHash`, `promptDraftBytes === specBytes`), the
  `runId`, and `binding: "prompt"`. An edited draft, another run's approval, or
  a missing field fails `AUTH_APPROVAL_STALE` / `AUTH_APPROVAL_INCOMPLETE`.
- `openGaps` must be `0` and the draft must contain no `[OPEN:` marker.
  `approve sign --allow-open` records a nonzero count, which the plan then
  refuses (`AUTH_APPROVAL_INCOMPLETE`).
- `approvalNonce` must be at least 128 bits, equal `_auth.nonce`, and unused for
  the run. The plugin consumes it once at plan time and stores
  `{approvalNonce, approvalDigest, planHash, at}` at
  `ctx.storage` `auth/approval/<runId>/consumed`; a later different nonce is
  `AUTH_APPROVAL_REPLAY`.
- `approvedAt`/`expiresAt` must be fresh. The default lifetime is 24 hours
  (`OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_APPROVAL_TTL_MS`, capped at 7 days); a stale, expired, or
  over-long approval fails `AUTH_APPROVAL_STALE`. A prompt-bound approval is
  produced before the plan, so it must still be live when the manifest was
  written.
- `approvedBy`/`attestedBy` must look like a principal: `uid:<name>`,
  `oidc:<issuer>#<sub>`, or `ci:<workflow>`. A bare `team/...` or `ses_...`
  label fails `AUTH_APPROVAL_NOT_HUMAN`.
- The plugin signer and any `command:` signer refuse an `approvals/` path with
  `AUTH_APPROVAL_SCOPE`. Approvals are produced only by
  `opencode-teamwork approve sign` (or an equivalent CI job) holding the
  approver private key directly.

This establishes that a **different configured principal signed these exact
draft bytes and this run while the approval was fresh**. It does **not**
establish that a human read the draft, understood it, or approves the
behaviour: the identity is a claimed label, not an identity proof, the CLI
cannot prove that the text displayed to the approver was the text hashed, and
approval content is not validated. The run process must still be configured so
that the approver key and directory are outside the agent's write reach; a
same-UID approver is not a boundary and cannot satisfy the gate.

> `human-approved` means the approval artifact verifies under an Ed25519 key
> the agent's process does not hold and cannot ask to sign, and is bound to the
> exact bytes of prompt_draft.md and this run. It does not establish that a
> human read the draft, that the displayed text matched the bytes hashed, or
> that the approver understood it. Treat it as provenance, not comprehension.

A new plan with `human-approved`/`ci-attested` refuses **before writing
anything** when the directory, approver key, draft, or approval is missing or
incomplete (`AUTH_APPROVAL_DIR` / `AUTH_APPROVAL_UNTRUSTED` /
`AUTH_APPROVAL_INCOMPLETE`). Manifests written by 0.10.1 and earlier
(version 1) keep their old in-run `approvals/<run>.json` path readable, but
`final_verify` records `approval_unbound` and does not claim a distinct
principal for it. Version 2 (0.10.2) keeps its manifestDigest-bound approval
semantics.

### CI attestation (`attestationPolicy`, 0.18.0)

`attestationPolicy` (`off` | `optional` | `required`, default `off`) is a
separate, post-plan requirement. A CI job holding an Ed25519 key the run does
not have signs `verify/ci/attestation.json` over the run nonce, plan hash,
prompt hash, commit and the argv/cwd/exit/output digest of every command it
ran. `final_verify` and `verify --attestation-public-key` bind it to the signed
manifest and every report head; a run-key signature is
`AUTH_ATTESTATION_UNTRUSTED`, and a foreign run id/nonce is
`AUTH_ATTESTATION_REPLAY`.

This establishes that **a second configured identity signed the same plan and
commit and observed the same command outputs**. It does not establish that the
suite is meaningful, that a test was not edited in the same commit, or that the
CI principal is independent of the agent's UID. Configure the verify-only key
with `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_ATTESTATION_PUBLIC_KEY`; the private key belongs only
to the CI producer. `doctor --security` fails `attestation_key` when private
material is visible to this process and warns when `attestationPolicy` is
`required` but no key is configured. See
[ADR 0018](docs/adr/0018-ci-attestation.md).

Benchmark integrity refuses an explicit `local-hmac` trust level and warns when
the default is used.

## Decision tree

1. **Single-user laptop, no separate privilege domain.** Use `local-hmac`
   (the default). Accept that a same-UID shell can forge verdicts. The envelope
   still stops run-dir-only writers, accidental copies, and post-plan
   downgrades.
2. **You need verification without giving the verifier the signing secret.**
   Use an Ed25519 key and publish only the SPKI public key
   (`OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_ED25519_PUBLIC_KEY`), or a command signer with
   `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER_PUBLIC_KEY`. Choose `external-signer`.
3. **You need a real boundary against the agent's UID.** Use the hardened
   profile: run the signer as a **separate OS user** (or a remote KMS/HSM) and
   give it a no-oracle policy — sign only after a human approves the exact
   `(runId, path, digest)`, or after an independent verifier recomputes the
   verdict from evidence the agent UID cannot rewrite. Pair it with
   `human-approved` or `ci-attested`, and configure a witness.
4. **You need post-hoc detection of index tampering.** Configure
   `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_WITNESS=command:<path>` or `http(s)://<url>` and set
   `requireWitness: true` on the plan. A witness receipt is appended on every
   signed write and checked by `final_verify` (`AUTH_WITNESS_UNAVAILABLE` when
   required and missing). Configure `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_WITNESS_PUBLIC_KEY` to
   make the receipt a signature over `(runId, path, digest, nonce, at)`: a
   forged KV receipt is then `AUTH_INVALID` instead of accepted. Without that
   public key the receipt is recorded and labelled `unverified` in
   `verify/final.json`; a local file/command witness is detection-only and
   shares the same UID either way.
5. **You need an observer outside the agent's process.** Run
   `.github/workflows/attest.yml` (or `scripts/attest-sign.mjs`) under a CI
   principal, set `attestationPolicy: "required"`, and give the verifier only
   `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_ATTESTATION_PUBLIC_KEY`. The attestation binds the signed
   plan, the report's commit and the command outputs to a key the run does not
   hold. It is only a boundary when the agent's UID cannot read the CI key.

The hardened profile is an administrator/deployment change (a system service,
separate UID, SELinux labels, or a remote approver). The plugin cannot create
that boundary in-process. The step-by-step administrator runbook is
[docs/ADMIN-HARDENING.md](docs/ADMIN-HARDENING.md); the policy-enforcing signer
contract is [docs/SIGNER-PROTOCOL.md](docs/SIGNER-PROTOCOL.md); the read-only
host verifier is [scripts/hardening-check.sh](scripts/hardening-check.sh). Those
steps are deployment guidance, not something the plugin enforces.

| `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER_PUBLIC_KEY` | SPKI public key used to verify the signer's response. Required. |
| `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER_KEY_ID` | Optional expected key id; defaults to a digest of the public key. |

| `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_WITNESS` | `command:<absolute path>` or `http(s)://<url>`. |

| `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_APPROVAL_DIR` | Absolute approval directory outside the run and repo, owned by a different UID. Required for `human-approved`/`ci-attested`. |
| `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_APPROVAL_PUBLIC_KEY` | SPKI Ed25519 public key of the approver (verify-only). Pinned as `approvalKeyId` at plan time. |

| `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_APPROVAL_KEY_FILE` | Path to a PEM or base64url PKCS#8 approver key for `approve sign` (alternative to the env/`--key`). |

The command signer receives `{v, alg, keyId, path, digest, nonce, at, message}`
when `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER_APPROVAL_DIR` is unset, or
`{v: 2, op: "sign-artifact", runId, alg, keyId, path, digest, nonce, at,
approvalRef, message}` when it is set, and must return
`{alg: "ed25519", keyId, sig}`. The plugin verifies the returned signature with
the configured public key before accepting it. A configured but unavailable,
malformed, timing-out, or non-verifying signer fails closed with
`AUTH_SIGNER_UNAVAILABLE`; it never falls back to the local HMAC key. A v1-only
signer with the directory set, or a v2-only signer without it, fails the same
way. The plugin derives `approvalRef` as
`<DIR>/<runId>/<plain sha256(path)>.json` and does not read the approval; the
signer's policy is outside the plugin.

## Residual risks

- **Offline verification is relational, not observational.** `opencode-teamwork
  verify` (0.15.0) recomputes the envelopes, evidence digests, citations,
  handoffs, branch binding and contradictions from a read-only copy and a public
  key. It cannot execute a claimed check, so an invented `output` with a correct
  `outputSha256` still verifies. A consistently authored false report passes
  every check. A whole-run rollback to an earlier signed set is undetectable
  without `--require-index <snapshot>` or an external witness. The exact
  residual is: a verifier holding only the public key and a read-only copy can
  recompute every byte digest, citation, branch binding and cross-artifact
  relation; it still cannot prove an observation, a consistently authored false
  report passes every check, and a whole-run rollback to an earlier signed set
  is undetectable without a snapshot or witness.
- **Re-execution narrows the residual; it does not close it.** Under
  `requiredProvenance: "command"` (0.16.0) a `PASS` must now survive
  `opencode-teamwork verify --rerun --repo <clean-checkout>`: the signed
  `verify/rerun.json` commands are re-executed at the report's commit in a
  disposable worktree and their exit code and output digest must match. The
  engine itself never runs the command (`teamwork_report` records the
  observation; `final_verify` only checks the record shape), so a compromised
  verifier can still author a consistent claim that the deployed environment
  later reproduces. A meaningless command (for example `true`), a test edited in
  the same commit, a non-deterministic command, or one whose output exceeds the
  bounded capture still passes; re-execution proves reproducibility of the
  recorded command at that commit, not that the command tests the requirement.
  `declared` runs keep the 0.15 residual unchanged.
- **Same-UID key access.** A local HMAC or Ed25519 private key is only as secret
  as the process UID. Only a different privilege domain (separate UID, KMS/HSM,
  hardware token) changes that.
- **Command signer is only non-oracle if external.** A signer reachable by the
  agent's UID can be called by any same-UID process. Its policy, not its
  location, is what makes it meaningful.
- **Nonce and index storage.** The nonce, key-id pin, and digest index live in
  plugin storage. A same-UID writer can rewrite them; the witness is the
  optional cross-check. A witness receipt is only `verified` when a witness
  public key is configured and its signature covers the run, path, digest,
  nonce and signed time. Without that key it is `unverified` (detection-only),
  and a local witness shares the UID.
- **Approval artifact.** `approvals/<runId>.json` is verified with the
  configured approval key. The plugin refuses to sign an `approvals/` path, and
  0.11.0 requires an Ed25519 approver key distinct from `runKeyId` and an
  approval directory owned by another UID. The approval proves which configured
  key signed which exact draft bytes and run id; it does not prove the
  approver's real-world identity, that a human read the draft, that the text
  displayed to the approver matched the bytes hashed, or that the approval
  content is accurate.
- **Approval content is a name, not a proof.** `approvedBy` is a claimed label.
  A compromised or careless approver process can sign any draft, and a
  same-UID key holder (including a single-UID sandbox) cannot satisfy the
  distinct-principal requirement at all. `doctor --security` now fails
  `approval_key` when the approver private key (inline or a readable key file)
  is visible to the workload UID, but a single-UID host cannot fix that by
  configuration. There is no human-presence enforcement: the CLI asks for a
  typed digest prefix and the word `approve`, but a script holding the key can
  reproduce both.
- **CI attestation is an identity claim plus a binding, not a proof of quality.**
  With `attestationPolicy: "required"` (0.18.0) the declared commands ran at the
  recorded commit under a separate signing identity, and the key is distinct
  from `runKeyId`; the attestation also binds the run nonce, plan hash, report
  head and command/output digests. It still does not prove the suite is
  meaningful, and a compromised CI, a weak suite, or a test edited in the same
  commit still pass. A CI principal reachable by the agent's UID (a repository
  secret readable from the workload, a key file in the same account) is not a
  boundary: the signature then proves the binding, not independence. The OIDC
  claims are checked only as a signed/pinned issuer string; no token is fetched
  or validated. A malicious dispatcher with write access to the protected
  branch can change what CI runs, which is exactly the CI privilege boundary
  the deployment must protect.
- **Display spoofing.** The CLI hashes the bytes on disk and prints the digest.
  It cannot prove that the approver's review surface showed those same bytes; a
  redirect, a different checkout, or a renderer that hides text is outside the
  boundary.

# Admin hardening runbook: a policy-enforcing signer

**Status:** deployment documentation for the 0.14.0 artifact-trust boundary.
This is a runbook for an administrator. **None of these steps was executed on
the host that wrote this document.** The commands are templates; substitute
your identities and paths, review every line, and test on a disposable host
first.

**The signer is not in this repository and is not shipped with the package.**
The plugin can call `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER=command:<path>` and, with a signer
approval directory, send a v2 request; the program at that path is yours. It
must be built (the outline and test list are in
[docs/SIGNER-PROTOCOL.md §8](SIGNER-PROTOCOL.md#8-reference-implementation-outline))
and installed as root-owned code in Step 7 below. Do not describe a deployment
as hardened because the plugin is configured; the signer's policy is the
boundary.

This runbook builds the deployment that the package cannot build in-process: a
signer in a different UID, root-owned signer code, a policy that refuses
arbitrary signing requests, OS controls that make the key harder to reach, and
detection for the remaining paths. It does not make the plugin, the prompts or
the model trustworthy. See [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md) for the boundary and
[docs/SIGNER-PROTOCOL.md](SIGNER-PROTOCOL.md) for the signer contract.

> **Version gate.** This runbook describes the **v2** policy signer. 0.14.0
> sends `v: 2` with `runId` and `approvalRef` only when
> `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER_APPROVAL_DIR` is set; without it the plugin sends
> the exact v1 request for back-compat. A v2-only signer will refuse a v1
> request, and the write fails `AUTH_SIGNER_UNAVAILABLE`; a v1-only signer with
> the directory set refuses the v2 request the same way. There is no fallback
> to the local HMAC key. Deploy the signer with the matching plugin, or keep
> the previous key source. Do not point a v1-only signer at a configured v2
> directory and call the result hardened.

> **What "policy-enforcing" means here.** A bare command signer that signs any
> well-formed `(path, digest)` is a signing oracle: a same-UID shell can ask it
> for the same signature the agent can. A policy-enforcing signer refuses to
> sign unless a separate principal has approved the exact run, path and digest,
> or unless the signer itself recomputes the verdict from evidence the agent
> cannot rewrite. The policy, not the socket permission, is the boundary.

---

## 1. Scope and threat model

### 1.1 What this runbook is meant to change

The base package's `local-hmac` and local-key modes are tamper-evident against a
writer limited to the run directory. They are not a boundary against a process
running as the agent's UID: that process can read `opencode.db` (or the plugin
KV store), read a local private key, mint an envelope, and rewrite the digest
index. A same-UID `command:` signer is callable by the same shell.

The hardened deployment in this runbook is intended to make the following
attacks fail **against an external verifier that trusts only the signer's public
key**:

| Attack | What the deployment changes |
| --- | --- |
| A same-UID shell reads the artifact key from `opencode.db` and mints a verdict | The verifier accepts only Ed25519 signatures from the signer key; the database key is not the signer key. |
| A run-directory writer forges or copies a signed verdict | Path, digest, run nonce, key id and signature are bound; the signer will not sign an unapproved digest. |
| A shell asks a command signer to sign an arbitrary `(path, digest)` | The v2 signer requires a separate approval bound to the exact `runId`, `path`, `digest`, `nonce` and expiry, and refuses without it. |
| The workload user reads the signer private key | The key is in a `0700` directory owned by the signer UID; `ptrace_scope=2` blocks same-UID memory access; the key is not in the environment. |
| The workload user replaces the signer executable | The signer and its client are root-owned, in a root-owned path, with no group/other write. |
| A forged approval file | The approval is an Ed25519 artifact owned by a different principal, opened with `O_NOFOLLOW`, and checked against the request. |

### 1.2 What it cannot change

- **A kernel exploit, root, `wheel`/`sudo`, or another root-equivalent group.**
  Root can read the key, ptrace the signer, edit the unit, and rewrite the audit
  log.
- **A compromised signer process or signer key.** The signer is the trust
  anchor. If it signs without its policy, or its key is stolen, the artifacts
  are signed by that key.
- **A compromised approver key or approval process.** The approval establishes
  that a configured key signed these fields. It does not establish that a human
  read the draft, that the displayed text matched the bytes hashed, or that the
  approver understood the consequence.
- **A prompt-injected agent.** The agent can still write false evidence, call
  tools, exfiltrate content, and ask for approval. The signer can refuse a
  signature for an unapproved digest; it cannot make the approved content true.
- **A modified plugin, config, prompt or model.** The plugin and
  `opencode.json` remain user-owned. A same-UID writer can disable the local
  gate. The external verifier and the signer's refusal are what remain. This
  runbook does not make the plugin trustworthy.
- **Availability and confidentiality.** The workload can delete runs, and run
  artifacts are not encrypted.
- **A human-presence proof.** The approval artifact is provenance for a
  configured key, not evidence that a person was present.

### 1.3 Trust boundary in one sentence

> A completion artifact is accepted by the external verifier only when it
> carries a signature from the signer key; the signer signs only after its
> policy checks the exact `(runId, path, digest, nonce)` against an approval
> owned by a different principal. Everything the workload UID can do before
> that point is still possible.

## 2. Preconditions

### 2.1 Accounts and access

1. **A separate administrator account** with working `sudo`. Do not use the
   workload account for administration, and do not use the human's daily login
   as the workload user.
2. **A workload user** that runs OpenCode and every agent. The recommended name
   is `opencode`. This user is the "agent UID" throughout this document.
3. **A signer user** (recommended `teamwork-signer`) that owns the signer key
   and runs the signer service. It is not the workload user and has no shell
   login.
4. **An approver user** (recommended `teamwork-approver`) that owns the
   approval directory and the approver private key. It is not the workload user
   and not the signer user.
5. **`openssl` 1.1.1 or later** on the host that creates the keys; `systemd`
   with socket activation; `auditd` (or an equivalent remote audit sink) if you
   want detection; SELinux tooling only if the host uses SELinux.

### 2.2 Values used below

Review and export these in your admin shell. They are examples, not a
requirement.

```sh

SIGNER_USER=teamwork-signer
APPROVER_USER=teamwork-approver

CLIENT_GROUP=teamwork-clients

### 2.3 Back up the current posture before changing anything

The backup is read-only output plus copies of the policy files. It is not a
secret backup: do not copy private keys into it.

```sh
umask 077
STAMP=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)
BACKUP=/var/backups/teamwork-posture-$STAMP
sudo install -d -m 0700 -o root -g root "$BACKUP"

# Policy files that a rollback may need.
sudo cp -a /etc/group /etc/gshadow "$BACKUP"/ 2>/dev/null || true
sudo cp -a /etc/sudoers "$BACKUP"/sudoers 2>/dev/null || true
sudo cp -a /etc/sysctl.d "$BACKUP"/sysctl.d 2>/dev/null || true
sudo cp -a /etc/audit/rules.d "$BACKUP"/audit-rules.d 2>/dev/null || true
sudo cp -a /etc/systemd/system "$BACKUP"/systemd-system 2>/dev/null || true
sudo cp -a /etc/fstab "$BACKUP"/fstab 2>/dev/null || true

# Read-only baseline: identities, groups, kernel, mounts, units, SELinux, audit.
{
  date -u
  printf '\n== id ==\n'; id
  printf '\n== workload identity ==\n'; getent passwd "$WORKLOAD_USER" || true
  printf '\n== workload groups ==\n'; id -Gn "$WORKLOAD_USER" 2>/dev/null || true
  printf '\n== root-equivalent groups ==\n'
  getent group root wheel sudo docker libvirt lxd disk adm systemd-journal 2>/dev/null || true
  printf '\n== ptrace ==\n'; sysctl -n kernel.yama.ptrace_scope 2>/dev/null || true
  printf '\n== /proc mount ==\n'; findmnt -no TARGET,OPTIONS /proc 2>/dev/null || true
  printf '\n== paths ==\n'
  stat -c '%A %a %U:%G %n' "$KEY_DIR" "$KEY_FILE" "$APPROVAL_DIR" "$SIGNER" "$PUBLIC_KEY" "$SOCKET" 2>&1 || true
  printf '\n== auditd ==\n'; systemctl show -p LoadState -p ActiveState auditd.service 2>/dev/null || true
  printf '\n== audit rules ==\n'; sudo auditctl -l 2>&1 || true
  printf '\n== SELinux ==\n'; getenforce 2>&1 || true
  printf '\n== units ==\n'
  sudo systemctl cat "$SOCKET_UNIT" "$SERVICE_UNIT" 2>&1 || true
  printf '\n== doctor (as workload, if installed) ==\n'
  sudo -u "$WORKLOAD_USER" sh -c 'command -v opencode-teamwork >/dev/null 2>&1 && opencode-teamwork doctor --security --json' 2>&1 || true
} | sudo tee "$BACKUP/baseline.txt" >/dev/null

sudo sha256sum "$BACKUP/baseline.txt" | sudo tee "$BACKUP/baseline.sha256" >/dev/null
sudo chmod 0600 "$BACKUP/baseline.txt" "$BACKUP/baseline.sha256"
```

**Proof.**

```sh
sudo test -s "$BACKUP/baseline.txt" && echo baseline-present
sudo sha256sum -c "$BACKUP/baseline.sha256"
sudo sed -n '1,60p' "$BACKUP/baseline.txt"
```

**Rollback.** Nothing was changed. Keep the directory until the deployment is
accepted; archive it if you need an audit trail. Delete it only with the
administrator's approval.

**Honest limit.** The baseline is a point-in-time read by a privileged process
on the host. A compromised kernel or a lying `sudo` can produce a false
baseline. The backup contains policy, not secrets; do not add private keys.

## 3. Step 1 — Capture and understand the baseline

**Purpose.** Establish what "before" means for every later rollback: UID/GID,
supplementary groups, socket modes, Yama `ptrace_scope`, `/proc` mount options,
`auditd` state, SELinux mode and the paths you are about to create.

**Commands.** Use the block in §2.3. Additionally record the exact facts the
verification script will later probe:

```sh
id
id -Gn
sysctl -n kernel.yama.ptrace_scope
findmnt -no OPTIONS /proc
systemctl show -p LoadState -p ActiveState auditd.service
getenforce 2>/dev/null || true
stat -c '%A %a %U:%G %n' /run /var/lib /etc 2>/dev/null || true
```

**Proof.** `id -u` is non-zero; `id -Gn` lists the groups you will change;
`sysctl -n` and `findmnt` return values or an empty/error line that you record;
`systemctl show` returns `LoadState` and `ActiveState`; `getenforce` returns
`Enforcing`, `Permissive`, `Disabled`, or an error (non-SELinux host).

**Rollback.** None; this step is read-only.

**Honest limit.** `id`, `sysctl`, `stat` and `systemctl` report the host's
current view. They do not prove that a process already running has the same
view, and they do not detect a kernel-level liar.

## 4. Step 2 — Remove root-equivalent groups from the workload user

**Purpose.** A member of `docker`, `libvirt`, `lxd`, `disk`, `adm` or
`systemd-journal` can often read the key, the database, the journal, or a block
device without becoming root. Remove those memberships from the workload user
before the signer exists.

`wheel` and `sudo` are a **policy decision**, not an automatic removal. If the
workload user can run arbitrary commands as root, no file mode in this runbook
matters. Removing `wheel`/`sudo` from the workload is recommended only when a
separate administrator account exists and the workload does not need
administrative commands. Otherwise, restrict `sudoers` and accept that the
workload is root-equivalent; the signer cannot fix that.

**Commands.**

```sh
# Show what is actually present before removing anything.
id -Gn "$WORKLOAD_USER"
getent group docker libvirt lxd disk adm systemd-journal 2>/dev/null || true
sudo -l -U "$WORKLOAD_USER" 2>/dev/null || true

# Remove the hard set. `gpasswd -d` fails on a primary group; do not remove a
# primary group here.
for g in docker libvirt lxd disk adm systemd-journal; do
  if id -nG "$WORKLOAD_USER" | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -qx "$g"; then
    sudo gpasswd -d "$WORKLOAD_USER" "$g"
  fi
done

# Policy decision only. Keep a separate admin account first.
# sudo gpasswd -d "$WORKLOAD_USER" wheel
# sudo gpasswd -d "$WORKLOAD_USER" sudo

# Terminate existing sessions so supplementary groups are not frozen.
sudo loginctl terminate-user "$WORKLOAD_USER" 2>/dev/null || true
```

**Proof.** A fresh login is required because supplementary groups are frozen in
existing processes. Do not trust a new shell started by the old process.

```sh
sudo -iu "$WORKLOAD_USER" -- id -Gn
sudo -n -u "$WORKLOAD_USER" -- id -Gn
```

Both must show the reduced set. Then inspect a running process's
`/proc/<pid>/status` `Groups:` line if any process survived; it still has the
old set until it is restarted. Restart OpenCode and its terminal (or reboot) and
re-check.

**Rollback.**

```sh
sudo gpasswd -a "$WORKLOAD_USER" docker     # repeat for each removed group
sudo loginctl terminate-user "$WORKLOAD_USER" 2>/dev/null || true
```

**Honest limit.** Group removal is not a complete privilege review. Check for
other root-equivalent paths: `podman` sockets, device ACLs, capabilities
(`getcap -r /` on the workload's binaries), sudoers rules with wildcards,
`/etc/sudoers.d`, polkit rules, and services that run commands on behalf of the
workload. `systemd-journal` removal can reduce log access; use an administrator
account or a scoped ACL rather than re-adding the workload. A process that is
already running keeps its old groups until it is restarted.

## 5. Step 3 — Set `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=2`

**Purpose.** Stop a same-UID process from attaching to the OpenCode or signer
process and reading its memory or environment. `ptrace_scope=1` is **not
enough** for this threat: Yama level 1 permits a process to trace its
**descendants**, and the shell that launched OpenCode is an ancestor. That shell
can therefore trace OpenCode under level 1. Level 2 permits only a process with
`CAP_SYS_PTRACE` (root/admin); level 3 disables attach entirely and is also
acceptable for a dedicated signer host, though it makes debugging harder.

**Commands.**

```sh
printf '%s\n' 'kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 2' \
  | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/90-teamwork-ptrace.conf >/dev/null
sudo chmod 0644 /etc/sysctl.d/90-teamwork-ptrace.conf
sudo sysctl --system
```

**Proof.** Start a disposable process as the workload user and attempt the two
reads as that same user.

```sh
sudo -u "$WORKLOAD_USER" sleep 300 &
TEST_PID=$!
sleep 0.2

sysctl -n kernel.yama.ptrace_scope
sudo -u "$WORKLOAD_USER" gdb -p "$TEST_PID" -batch -ex 'info proc' 2>&1 || true
sudo -u "$WORKLOAD_USER" cat "/proc/$TEST_PID/mem" >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "mem_exit=$?"
sudo -u "$WORKLOAD_USER" head -c 1 "/proc/$TEST_PID/environ" >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "environ_exit=$?"

kill "$TEST_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
```

Expected: the `gdb` attach fails with an operation-not-permitted error (or
`gdb` is absent), `mem_exit` is non-zero, and **`environ_exit` is 0**. That last
result is the honest limit: `/proc/<pid>/environ` remains readable by the same
UID even with `ptrace_scope=2`. Keys must not live in environment

**Generate the signer key as the signer UID, not as root and not as the
workload.**

```sh
sudo -u "$SIGNER_USER" sh -c 'umask 077; openssl genpkey -algorithm ED25519 -out "$1"' sh "$KEY_FILE"
sudo chmod 0600 "$KEY_FILE"

# SPKI public key, base64url (no padding), mode 0644.
sudo -u "$SIGNER_USER" openssl pkey -in "$KEY_FILE" -pubout -outform DER \

  | sudo tee "$PUBLIC_KEY" >/dev/null
sudo chmod 0644 "$PUBLIC_KEY"
```

**Generate the approver key as the approver UID.**

```sh
sudo -u "$APPROVER_USER" sh -c 'umask 077; openssl genpkey -algorithm ED25519 -out "$1"' sh "$APPROVER_KEY_DIR/approver.pem"
sudo chmod 0600 "$APPROVER_KEY_DIR/approver.pem"

sudo -u "$APPROVER_USER" openssl pkey -in "$APPROVER_KEY_DIR/approver.pem" -pubout -outform DER \
  | openssl base64 -A | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=' \
  | sudo tee "$APPROVER_PUBLIC_KEY" >/dev/null
sudo chmod 0644 "$APPROVER_PUBLIC_KEY"
```

**Approval file modes.** The shipped `approve sign` CLI writes its prompt
approval with mode `0600` (ADR 0011), but the workload must read that file for
the `human-approved` trust level. After producing it, the approver must make it
group-readable without making it writable:

```sh
# Prompt approval (human-approved/ci-attested); run as the approver.
RUN_ID=r-01J8Z5K8V6Q9W2M4N7P3S6T8X0
PROMPT_APPROVAL="$APPROVAL_DIR/$RUN_ID.json"
chgrp "$APPROVAL_GROUP" "$PROMPT_APPROVAL"
chmod 0640 "$PROMPT_APPROVAL"
```

For a v2 signer approval, the signer (not the workload) must read the file. The
layout is **one file per `(runId, path)`**, derived by both the producer and the
plugin from trusted inputs:

```text
$SIGNER_APPROVAL_DIR/<runId>/<sha256(run-relative path)>.json
```

The hash is a **plain SHA-256** of the UTF-8 path (`contentSha256Hex` in
`plugins/opencode-teamwork/approval-format.mjs`), not the keyed artifact digest.
Put the file in the separate subdirectory and give it the signer-approval group:

```sh
# Example after producing one signer approval with `approve signer`; run as the approver.
RUN_ID=r-01J8Z5K8V6Q9W2M4N7P3S6T8X0
PATH_HASH=$(printf '%s' "verify/victory.json" | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1)
SIGNER_APPROVAL_FILE="$SIGNER_APPROVAL_DIR/$RUN_ID/$PATH_HASH.json"
chgrp "$SIGNER_APPROVAL_GROUP" "$SIGNER_APPROVAL_FILE"
chmod 0640 "$SIGNER_APPROVAL_FILE"
```

Read access is required for verification and is not the boundary; write access
is. Do not make either directory `0770`, and do not add the workload to
`teamwork-signer-approvals`.

**Proof.**

```sh
stat -c '%A %a %U:%G %n' "$KEY_DIR" "$KEY_FILE" "$APPROVER_KEY_DIR" \
  "$APPROVAL_DIR" "$SIGNER_APPROVAL_DIR" "$PUBLIC_KEY" "$APPROVER_PUBLIC_KEY"

sudo -u "$WORKLOAD_USER" test -r "$KEY_FILE";  echo "workload_key_read=$?"   # expect 1
sudo -u "$WORKLOAD_USER" test -r "$APPROVAL_DIR"; echo "workload_approval_read=$?" # expect 0
sudo -u "$WORKLOAD_USER" test -w "$APPROVAL_DIR"; echo "workload_approval_write=$?" # expect 1
sudo -u "$WORKLOAD_USER" test -r "$SIGNER_APPROVAL_DIR"; echo "workload_signer_approval_read=$?" # expect 1
sudo -u "$SIGNER_USER" test -r "$SIGNER_APPROVAL_DIR"; echo "signer_approval_read=$?" # expect 0
sudo -u "$SIGNER_USER" test -r "$APPROVER_PUBLIC_KEY"; echo "signer_pub_read=$?" # expect 0
id -nG "$WORKLOAD_USER" | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -x "$SIGNER_APPROVAL_GROUP" && echo "BAD: workload in signer-approval group" || true
```

**Rollback.**

```sh
# Archive keys and approvals first. Deleting the signer key stops new
# signatures; old signatures remain verifiable with the archived public key.
sudo gpasswd -d "$WORKLOAD_USER" "$APPROVAL_GROUP" 2>/dev/null || true
sudo gpasswd -d "$WORKLOAD_USER" "$SIGNER_APPROVAL_GROUP" 2>/dev/null || true
sudo userdel "$SIGNER_USER" 2>/dev/null || true
sudo userdel "$APPROVER_USER" 2>/dev/null || true
sudo groupdel "$SIGNER_GROUP" 2>/dev/null || true
sudo groupdel "$CLIENT_GROUP" 2>/dev/null || true
sudo groupdel "$APPROVAL_GROUP" 2>/dev/null || true
sudo groupdel "$SIGNER_APPROVAL_GROUP" 2>/dev/null || true
sudo rm -rf "$KEY_DIR" "$APPROVER_KEY_DIR" "$APPROVAL_DIR" /etc/teamwork
```

**Honest limit.** A different owner and a `0700`/`0750` mode are necessary but
not sufficient. The workload is in the prompt-approval group so it can read the
file it must verify; read access is not write access, but it does mean the
approval contents are visible to the workload. The signer is in both approval
groups and can read every approval it is asked to check; a compromised signer
can misuse that. The approver key holder can sign any approval; a script with
the key can reproduce the CLI's typed confirmation. The approval directory
owner is a claimed deployment fact, not an identity proof. The key file is only
as secret as the signer UID; root can read it.

## 9. Step 7 — Install root-owned signer code

**Purpose.** A signer executable that the workload can write is replaceable: the
workload can substitute a program that reads the request, ignores the policy,
and returns a signature. Root-owned code in a root-owned path removes that
specific path. It does **not** make the local plugin trustworthy; a same-UID
writer can still edit the plugin to call a different path, which is why the
external verifier must pin the public key.

**Commands.**

```sh
sudo install -d -m 0755 -o root -g root /usr/local/libexec/teamwork
sudo install -m 0755 -o root -g root ./target/release/teamwork-signer "$SIGNER"
sudo install -m 0755 -o root -g root ./signer-client "$CLIENT"
sudo chown root:root /usr/local/libexec/teamwork "$SIGNER" "$CLIENT"
sudo chmod 0755 /usr/local/libexec/teamwork "$SIGNER" "$CLIENT"

# No parent may be writable by the workload or by group/other.
namei -l "$SIGNER"
```

The client is a transport, not a policy. It must be root-owned so the workload
cannot replace it to lie about a signature. A malicious client can deny service
or replay bytes; it cannot forge a signature that the plugin verifies against
the pinned public key.

**Proof.**

```sh
stat -c '%A %a %U:%G %n' "$SIGNER" "$CLIENT"
namei -l "$SIGNER"
sudo -u "$WORKLOAD_USER" test -w "$SIGNER"; echo "workload_signer_write=$?" # expect 1
find /usr/local/libexec/teamwork -maxdepth 1 \( -perm -002 -o -perm -020 \) -print # expect no output
```

**Rollback.** Restore the previous binary from the baseline or package
manager, or remove the files. Do not leave a user-writable copy earlier in
`PATH`; the plugin uses an absolute path, but an operator command may not.

**Honest limit.** Root-owned code does not stop root, a package manager, or a
root compromise. It does not stop a same-UID writer from editing the
user-owned plugin, the agent prompts, or `opencode.json`; the local gate can be
disabled. It does not stop the workload from calling the signer socket, which
is intended. The external verifier's public-key pin and the signer's policy are
the remaining checks. A signer whose key is in an environment variable readable
by the workload is not protected by root-owned code.

## 15. Rollback order (reverse of the deployment)

Roll back in reverse dependency order: stop the thing that uses a path before
removing the path. There is one deliberate exception to a strict numeric
reverse: remove the audit rules **before** deleting the watched key, approval
and signer paths, because `augenrules --load` refuses a watch on a missing path.

1. **Verification (step 10):** nothing to roll back.
2. **SELinux (step 9):** remove the custom module and fcontext entries, then
   `restorecon`; do not use `setenforce 0`.
3. **Units (step 8):** disable the socket, stop instances, remove the unit
   files, `daemon-reload`, `reset-failed`, remove `/run/teamwork-signer`.
4. **Signer code (step 7):** restore the previous binaries or remove them; do
   not leave a user-writable copy.
5. **Audit (step 5):** remove the rules file and reload **before** deleting the
   watched paths; export the log first if it is evidence.
6. **Users/directories (step 6):** archive keys and approvals, then remove the
   users/groups and directories. Keep the public keys and old signatures for
   verification.
7. **hidepid (step 4):** remount with the baseline options and remove the
   `fstab` line.
8. **ptrace (step 3):** remove the sysctl file and restore the baseline value.
9. **Groups (step 2):** re-add only the groups the workload actually needs,
   then terminate sessions and log in again.

### If you must undo

Remove the signer configuration from the workload first: point it back at its
previous key source, or unset `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER`. A configured but
unavailable signer fails every signed write closed.

```sh
# 9. SELinux (only if you added the module/labels).
sudo semodule -r teamwork_signer 2>/dev/null || true
sudo semanage fcontext -d "$SIGNER" 2>/dev/null || true

**If you must undo, read this first.**

- **Remove the signer configuration before you disable the service.** A
  configured but unavailable signer fails every signed write closed with
  `AUTH_SIGNER_UNAVAILABLE`; that is by design, not a bug. Point the plugin back
  at its previous key source, or unset `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER`, before the
  service goes away.
- **Do not delete the public keys.** Old artifacts verify with the public key
  after the private key is gone. Deleting the public key removes the ability to
  verify history.
- **A rollback does not un-sign artifacts.** Artifacts already signed remain
  valid to a verifier that trusts the signer key. If you rotate or discard the
  key, update the verifier's trust store deliberately.
- **Restoring group membership needs a fresh login.** Running processes retain
  the old supplementary groups; `loginctl terminate-user` or a reboot is the
  reliable reset.
- **Restoring `ptrace_scope=0` reopens memory/environment exposure.** Do it
  only because you are returning to the lower-assurance profile, not as a
  debugging shortcut.
- **Removing audit rules removes detection.** Export or forward the audit log
  before deleting rules if it is evidence.
- **Do not use `setenforce 0` as a rollback.** Fix the label or remove the
  custom policy; permissive mode hides the problem.
- **A signer policy is not undone by removing a unit.** Approvals and signatures
  remain. If the approval private key was compromised, rotate the approver key
  and re-issue approvals; removing the service does not make old approvals
  invalid.

## 16. What this runbook still does not verify

- That the signer binary is the reviewed binary. Root-owned code is not a
  reproducible-build proof; compare a hash or signature out of band.
- That the signer's policy is correct. Read the source and run the tests in
  [SIGNER-PROTOCOL.md](SIGNER-PROTOCOL.md).
- That the approval key holder is a human, or that the human read the bytes.
- That the plugin, prompts, model or external verifier are unmodified.
- That an artifact accepted today is still true tomorrow. Re-execution and
  external review remain necessary.

**Again: no step in this document was executed on the documentation host.**

# Teamwork artifacts

Single source of truth for the files every Teamwork run reads and writes, and
for the topologies the coordinator may pick. Agents reference this file instead
of redefining formats.

## Layout

Every run writes under one root:

├── requirements.json        # plan-time requirements baseline (caller or request-derived; absent when neither exists)
├── run.manifest.json        # signed baseline: modes + request/requirements/plan/policy hashes (_auth)

`<session-id>` = `YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS-<4 hex>`.

Worktrees are created **outside the repository** (nested git worktrees inside
