## Topologies

| Topology | Shape |
| --- | --- |
| `small-focused` | 1 worker + 1 verifier loop |
| `iterative-coding` | 1 worker, test-driven tight loop on one module |
| `distributed-coding` | N workers fan-out + merge |
| `proof` | 1 strategist + 3-5 searchers + 1 formal checker (plus explicit opt-in LEMMA / Lean 4 mode via `lemmaMode: true`) |
| `massive-proof` | Bounded multi-level tournament search + falsers + mergers + referee (explicit opt-in only; 1 meta-coordinator + up to 100+ searchers) |
| `document-review` | segment triage (1–8 segments, default 6) → bounded per-segment RSA tree `[4,2,1]` → cross-segment synthesis `[4,1]` |

Legacy aliases — accept them, normalize on write:
`large-swarm` → `distributed-coding`, `doc-review` → `document-review`,
`long-proof` → `proof`, `massive-proof-swarm` → `massive-proof`.

## Integrity modes

Every run is routed with one integrity mode. It is recorded in
`ORIGINAL_REQUEST.md`, copied to `state.json` and `plan.dag.json`, and read back
by the security auditor and the final-verification gate from
`ORIGINAL_REQUEST.md` (never from the caller). The orchestrator records and
reports it; the auditor reports rule violations and the audit tool makes them
binding (see [Integrity rules](#integrity-rules)).

| Mode | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `development` | Default. Reuse, libraries and frameworks are allowed; only fabricated outputs and facade implementations are ruled out. |
| `demo` | Also forbids copying core logic from open source, delegating core work to external tools, and reading test sources to reverse-engineer expected behaviour. |
| `benchmark` | A fully independent from-scratch implementation using the language standard library only. |

`development` is the default: `teamwork_plan` applies it when `integrityMode` is
omitted, and the auditor and final gate apply it to legacy runs with no
`ORIGINAL_REQUEST.md`. Any other value is refused before anything is written.

### Integrity rules

The auditor reports structured integrity claims as `integrityFindings` on
`teamwork_security_audit`. Each rule is forbidden from a given mode onward, and
every stricter mode inherits it:

| Rule | Forbidden from |
| --- | --- |
| `fabricated_output` | `development` (always blocking) |
| `core_logic_copied` | `demo` |
| `delegated_core_work` | `demo` |
| `test_source_read` | `demo` |
| `external_dependency_used` | `benchmark` |

A finding whose rule is forbidden at the run's mode is a **violation**. Any
violation forces the audit to `FAIL` regardless of severity counts, so
`teamwork_final_verify` cannot reach `PASS` and the merge stays blocked; the
audit result names the violated rules and the mode. An unknown rule id is
refused before anything is written.

**Limitation.** The tool cannot detect dishonesty. It does not inspect the code
to prove a rule was broken; it takes the auditor's report at face value and
makes a reported violation binding on the gate.

## Schemas

### `ORIGINAL_REQUEST.md` — verbatim routed request (write-once)

`teamwork_plan` writes this file once, **before** `plan.dag.json` and
`state.json`, when its optional `request` input is provided. It is the artifact
the auditor reads the integrity mode from, and the path to hand any auditor that
checks the work against the original request.

- **Write-once.** If the file already exists with non-empty content, a second
  plan into the same run is refused ("write-once ... use a new session") and
  writes nothing else.
- **Verbatim.** The request text is preserved exactly — no reflow, no trimming
  of interior whitespace — and capped at 20,000 characters. A longer request is
  refused, never silently truncated.
- **Legacy tolerance.** When `request` is omitted, no file is created; the run
  still plans and the mode defaults to `development`.

Format:

~~~markdown
# Original Request

- Integrity mode: demo
- Recorded: 2026-01-12T10:15:00.000Z
- Session: 20260112-101500-a1b2

## Request

<verbatim request>
~~~

### `requirements.json` — plan-time requirements baseline

`teamwork_plan` writes this once per run when the caller supplies
`requirements`, or derives a single `R1` item from a supplied verbatim
`request`. When neither exists (legacy/tiny path), no file is written and the
plan records `victoryAudit: "skip"` explicitly.

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "source": "caller|request",
  "items": [{ "id": "R1", "text": "Behaviour-focused requirement" }]
}
```

- `source: "caller"` — the exact validated `requirements` array (order kept).
- `source: "request"` — one `R1` item containing the request text (≤2,000 chars).
- **Immutable once written.** A re-plan with a different baseline is refused;
  the same baseline is idempotent. This stops a confirmed verdict from being
  invalidated by editing the requirements afterwards.

### `run.manifest.json` — signed completion baseline (ADR 0005)

Written by `teamwork_plan` for a signed run (the default). It pins the run's
modes and the hashes a later gate recomputes, so a control-plane downgrade is
`AUTH_STALE` rather than accepted:

```json
{
  "version": 3,
  "sessionId": "20261122-120000-abcd",
  "rootSessionId": "ses_...",
  "integrityMode": "development|demo|benchmark",
  "verification": "standard|strict",
  "victoryAudit": "required|skip",
  "victorySkipReason": "why an explicit victory skip was recorded (only when skip)",
  "requireHandoffs": "required|skip",
  "handoffAuth": "signed|legacy",
  "requiredProvenance": "declared|command",
  "attestationPolicy": "off|optional|required",
  "attestationKeyId": "attestation_... | null",
  "attestationIssuer": "https://issuer | null",
  "requestHash": "sha256 | null",
  "requirementsHash": "sha256 | null",
  "planHash": "sha256",
  "lemmaPolicyHash": "sha256 | null",
  "runKeyId": "k_...",
  "trustLevel": "local-hmac|external-signer|human-approved|ci-attested",
  "requireWitness": false,
  "approvalPolicy": "external-dir|in-run-legacy|none",
  "approvalKeyId": "approval_... | null",
  "specHash": "sha256 of the exact prompt_draft.md bytes | null",
  "specBytes": 2089,
  "approvalDigest": "sha256 of the approval payload without _auth | null",
  "approvalNonce": "base64url >=128-bit one-use nonce | null",
  "approvalBinding": "prompt",
  "approvedBy": "uid:<name>|oidc:<issuer>#<sub>|ci:<workflow> | null",
  "approvedAt": "2026-11-22T11:59:00.000Z",
  "createdAt": "2026-11-22T12:00:00.000Z",
  "_auth": {
    "v": 1,
    "alg": "hmac-sha256",
    "keyId": "k_...",
    "path": "run.manifest.json",
    "digest": "sha256",
    "mac": "sha256",
    "at": "2026-11-22T12:00:00.000Z"
  }
}
```

- Version 3 is written by 0.11.0+. Version 2 (0.10.2) and version 1
  (pre-0.10.2) manifests remain readable. Version 1 in-run
  `approvals/<runId>.json` is honoured only for those runs and is recorded as
  `approval_unbound`; version 2 keeps its manifestDigest-bound approval
  semantics. Version 4 (0.16.0+) adds `requiredProvenance`; versions 1–3 are
  read as `declared`. A re-plan may upgrade `declared → command` but never
  downgrade it (`AUTH_STALE`). Version 5 (0.18.0+) adds the CI attestation
  policy and pins; versions 1–4 are read as `attestationPolicy: "off"`.
- `specHash` is an **unkeyed SHA-256 of the exact file bytes** (not the keyed
  artifact digest), and `specBytes` is the byte length. `teamwork_plan` reads
  the draft through the bounded no-follow run reader before any `mkdir`, so a
  symlinked, non-regular, or edited draft cannot be planned against a different
  text. A version-3 plan records `specHash`/`specBytes` whenever a draft exists,
  including `local-hmac` runs; editing the draft later is `AUTH_STALE`.
- `approvalPolicy`/`approvalKeyId`/`specHash`/`specBytes`/`approvalDigest`/
  `approvalNonce`/`approvalBinding`/`approvedBy`/`approvedAt` are part of the
  signed baseline and drift checks. `human-approved`/`ci-attested` pin
  `external-dir` and the configured verify-only approver key; a re-plan cannot
  remove or change either. For a version-3 approval, the manifest records the
  approval payload digest (never a digest of the manifest inside the approval),
  which removes the old circular manifestDigest requirement.

- `rootSessionId` is the plan-time caller session. `teamwork_victory_audit`,
  `teamwork_wave_record`, and `teamwork_report` require the caller session to
  be a strict descendant of it (walked through `parentID`, bounded, fail closed).
- `planHash` covers the semantic plan (topology, modes, the victory skip reason
  when present, route, LEMMA bounds, tasks), not formatting or `routingReason`.
- An explicit `victoryAudit: "skip"` requires `victorySkipReason` (non-empty,
  trimmed, ≤500 chars, sanitized). The reason is persisted in
  `plan.dag.json`, `state.json` and this manifest; a re-plan may repeat it but
  not change it (`AUTH_STALE`). The legacy no-baseline default skip has no
  reason and is labelled `SKIPPED (legacy default: no requirements baseline)`.
- A re-plan must present the same modes and hashes. `final_verify`/`next`
  return `AUTH_STALE` if `plan.dag.json`, `state.json`, `ORIGINAL_REQUEST.md`,
  `requirements.json`, or the LEMMA policy diverges from the manifest.
- `handoffAuth` pins the handoff-index provenance baseline. A new signed plan
  writes `"signed"`; a plan created with `allowUnsignedLegacy: true` writes
  `"legacy"`; a 0.8.0 manifest without the field is read as `"legacy"`. A
  re-plan may upgrade `legacy → signed`, but a `signed → legacy` downgrade is
  `AUTH_STALE` and refused.
- `requiredProvenance` is the re-execution requirement (0.16.0). `declared`
  (the default, and the meaning of versions 1–3) means a PASS report's checks
  are authenticated but not re-executed. `command` means every `PASS` report
  must carry at least one `type: "programmatic"` check with an argv-only
  `command`, a `cwd`, an `exitCode`, an untruncated output digest, and a
  `headSha`; the engine writes a signed `verify/rerun.json`, and
  `opencode-teamwork verify --rerun --repo <clean-checkout>` re-executes it
  before a verdict can be `PASS`. A re-plan may upgrade to `command` but a
  downgrade is `AUTH_STALE`.
- `attestationPolicy`/`attestationKeyId`/`attestationIssuer` are the CI
  attestation requirement (0.18.0). `off` (the default and the meaning of
  versions 1–4) ignores `verify/ci/attestation.json`; `optional` records its
  status without failing the run; `required` refuses completion without a
  valid artifact. A re-plan may upgrade `off → optional → required`, never
  downgrade, and cannot change a pinned key id or issuer (`AUTH_STALE`).
- **Legacy:** `allowUnsignedLegacy: true` at plan time creates/keeps an
  unsigned run. Its completion gates return `AUTH_LEGACY` until the caller
  explicitly passes `allowUnsignedLegacy: true`; that bypass is recorded as a
  `legacy_unsigned_bypass` event. An unsigned baseline cannot require the
  handoff gate, so it records `requireHandoffs: "skip"`. `benchmark` refuses the
  bypass and refuses both `victoryAudit: "skip"` and `requireHandoffs: "skip"`.

Written by `teamwork_preflight` for an existing run (`teamwork_plan` records

```json
  "integrityMode": "development",
  "items": [
    { "value": "/abs/path/spec.md", "kind": "path", "blocking": true, "advisory": false, "status": "READY", "detail": "file" },
    { "value": "docs/draft.md", "kind": "path", "blocking": false, "advisory": true, "status": "MISSING" },
    { "value": "https://example.com/issue/1", "kind": "url", "blocking": true, "advisory": false, "status": "UNCHECKED", "detail": "checkUrls: false" }
```

### `costs.json`

```json
{
  "sessionId": "...",
  "budgetUsd": 20,
  "budgetSource": "credits|default|manual",
  "spentUsd": 0,
  "byTask": {},
  "byTaskTokens": {},
  "appliedSnapshotDigest": "sha256 hex of the last applied usage observation",
  "appliedSnapshotAt": "ISO8601",
  "snapshotCursors": {
    "ses_abc123": {
      "lastCost": 0.62,
      "lastTokens": { "input": 1200, "output": 640, "reasoning": 0, "cache": { "read": 300, "write": 40 } },
      "agent": "team/sentinel",
      "timestamp": "ISO8601"
    }
  },
  "lastCostUpdate": {
    "at": "ISO8601",
    "source": "opencode session tree (...)",
    "digest": "sha256 hex",
    "skippedDuplicate": false
  },
  "updatedAt": "ISO8601"
}
```

`appliedSnapshotDigest` is the idempotency key for native snapshot updates. The
digest is a stable sha256 over the observed session id, agent, cost, and token
totals. When `teamwork_cost` observes the **same** digest again (for example a
retry after the process crashed between the costs write and the snapshots write,
or an immediate second call), it adds no cost/token delta and records
`lastCostUpdate.skippedDuplicate: true`. `snapshotCursors` is the authoritative
per-session delta baseline; `snapshots.json` remains a compatibility view and is
refreshed after `costs.json`, but a missing/stale copy cannot double-count.
Manual `addUsd` calls have no snapshot digest and are recorded without touching
either digest or cursors.

`byTask` maps a bucket name to its cumulative spend in USD. `byTaskTokens` is an
additive key (added after the original schema) keyed by bucket name. Both are
updated in the same locked section, but their key sets are **not** guaranteed to
be identical: every `byTaskTokens` key is also a `byTask` key, while a `byTask`
bucket can have spend and no `byTaskTokens` entry (see the all-zero case below):

```json
{
  "byTask":       { "R1-impl": 0.1234 },
  "byTaskTokens": { "R1-impl": { "input": 1200, "output": 640, "reasoning": 0, "cache": { "read": 300, "write": 40 } } }
}
```

Each `byTaskTokens` bucket holds integer token deltas (current session totals
minus the per-session `lastTokens` recorded in `costs.snapshotCursors`, mirrored
in `snapshots.json`), the same way cost deltas are computed. A `costs.json`
without `byTaskTokens` is valid: readers treat it as absent. The manual `addUsd`
path has no token data, so it adds dollars to `byTask` only and leaves
`byTaskTokens` untouched. The session-global `tokens` total is unchanged.

A token delta whose five components are all zero (for example, a session whose
cost rose but whose tokens did not change) is skipped **before** either map is
touched. In that case the bucket still gains its spend in `byTask` but gets no
`byTaskTokens` key. Readers must treat a missing `byTaskTokens[<bucket>]` as "no
token data", not as zero.

**Bucket names are safe map keys.** A `taskId` must match
`^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,63}$`. Both `teamwork_plan` (task ids and
`dependsOn`) and `teamwork_cost` (`taskId`) refuse anything else, so ids such as
`__proto__` or `a/b` are never stored. `byTask`, `byTaskTokens` and `state.tasks`
are null-prototype maps in memory, so an id such as `constructor` is an ordinary
key. The allowlist is the guard; `clean()` alone does not prevent these ids.

**Bucketing rule.** Each session in the run's tree is assigned a bucket when
`teamwork_cost` finds spend for it:

1. The calling session, when `taskId` is supplied → `taskId`.
2. A root session (the run's sentinel) → `taskId` if supplied, else `_sentinel`.
3. Any other (non-root, e.g. worker or verifier) session → `taskId` if supplied,
   else its agent name (the legacy behaviour), else `_unattributed`.

So when the sentinel calls `teamwork_cost({ taskId })` at a task boundary, the
spend of the worker and verifier sessions lands on **that task**. Without a
`taskId`, subagent spend is still bucketed by agent name, exactly as before.

**Per-task attribution requires the sentinel to call it.** Per-task cost and
tokens only populate for runs whose sentinel called `teamwork_cost({ taskId })`
after each worker return and each verifier report. Spend recorded by calls made
without a `taskId` stays in agent-name or `_sentinel` buckets.

**Timeline `tokens`.** The timeline view (`lib/timeline.mjs`) reports each task's
`tokens` as `costs.byTaskTokens[<taskId>]`, when that bucket exists and holds
finite numbers. It is `null` otherwise, and **always `null` for any run recorded
before `byTaskTokens` existed**. Per-task token counts are not reconstructed for
older runs.

When the session uses `opencode/` (managed) models and the `opencode_console`
MCP is connected, `teamwork_budget` tells the sentinel to derive `budgetUsd`
from console credits (`opencode_console_get_usage` →
`min(limitDollars - spentDollars)`), after asking the user whether to use the
full remaining budget or a partial (half) amount. `budgetSource` records where
the budget came from.

**The budget is advisory outside the massive-proof tournament.** `teamwork_cost`
warns when floored usage reaches 80% of a positive `budgetUsd` and returns
`shouldHalt: true` plus the explicit `thresholdPct: 80`; the Sentinel is
expected to halt non-essential workers and ask the user. No standard-run tool
refuses work on that signal: `teamwork_next` can still lease a ready task,
`teamwork_task_update` can start another round, and `teamwork_final_verify` can
still stamp a verdict. The only enforced budget is the tournament preflight and
dispatch halt described under [Tournament artifacts](#tournament-artifacts-massive-proof-explicit-opt-in),
which writes `BUDGET_HALTED` and a `PRESENT_PARTIAL` report. `budgetUsd: 0` is
an explicit no-budget run: `teamwork_cost` reports 0% and never returns
`shouldHalt`, and a standard run keeps dispatching. A missing `budgetUsd` key is
not the same as `0`; a new plan resolves it to the default budget.

Cost and token consumption are read directly from OpenCode, not self-reported.
The engine discovers the full OpenCode session tree rooted at the run's sentinel
session (`opencode.db` SQLite tree query, background service API, or client get),
aggregating the root session and all child/subagent sessions (workers, verifiers,
scouts, auditors). Deltas between calls are tracked by the auth

### Re-execution (`--rerun`, 0.16.0)

`--rerun` needs `--repo <clean-checkout>` and a recorded `verify/rerun.json`.
For each check it creates a detached worktree at the report's `headSha`, runs
the recorded argv with `spawnSync` (no shell, a minimal environment, `cwd`
inside the worktree), enforces `timeoutMs` (capped by `--timeout <s>`), and
compares the exit code and the unkeyed sha256 of stdout+stderr to the recorded
values. `sh -c`/`bash -c` and a `cwd` that escapes the worktree are refused.
The source checkout is hashed before and after and a change is
`source-tree-modified`. The worktree is removed unless `--keep-worktree`.

| Outcome | Exit | Code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| exit 0 and digest match | 0 | `PASS` |
| output digest or byte count changed | 1 | `output-digest-mismatch` |
| re-executed exit is non-zero (or differs from `expectedExit`) | 1 | `command-failed` |
| binary cannot be executed (ENOENT/EACCES) | 2 | `command-unavailable` |
| `timeoutMs` exceeded | 1 | `command-timeout` |
| shell line or escaping `cwd` | 1 | `command-refused` |

Under `requiredProvenance: "command"`, `verify` without `--rerun` reports the
claim as `provenance: claimed` and returns `UNKNOWN`, never `PASS`. Under
`declared` the 0.15 behaviour is unchanged, with a `provenance: declared` note;
`--rerun` can still be used opportunistically.

### Exit codes and JSON

`0` verified (`PASS`), `1` fail (`FAIL`), `2` unverifiable (`UNKNOWN`), `3`
usage. `--fail-on-warning` promotes a warning to exit 1. `--json` prints the
stable object described in ADR 0015; the human table is rendered from it.
`--allow-unsigned` analyses an unsigned legacy run but the verdict stays
`UNKNOWN`: a missing signature is exactly what the verifier cannot supply.

Since 0.18.0 `--json` also carries `attestation: {status, commitSha, keyId,
issuer}` and `attested: boolean`. Without `--attestation-public-key` a present
attestation is `UNKNOWN` (exit 2) and is never promoted to `PASS`; under
`required` a supplied key turns a missing artifact into `FAIL`
(`AUTH_ATTESTATION_MISSING`) and a bad one into its named code.

### Index snapshot (`--require-index`)

A per-artifact check cannot see a whole-run rollback to an earlier validly
signed set. A snapshot maps each run-relative file to its unkeyed SHA-256:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "runId": "20261124-120000-abcd",
  "generatedAt": "2026-11-24T12:06:00.000Z",
  "files": { "run.manifest.json": "<sha256>", "verify/report-R1.json": "<sha256>" }
}
```

Every snapshot file must still match, and every current run file must be in the
snapshot. A difference is `INDEX_ROLLBACK` (exit 1). `--require-index` without a
path is `UNKNOWN` (exit 2). The snapshot is caller-supplied, not signed by this
tool.

### What it cannot prove

A verifier holding only the public key and a read-only copy can recompute every
byte digest, citation, branch binding and cross-artifact relation; it still
cannot prove an observation, a consistently authored false report passes every
check, and a whole-run rollback to an earlier signed set is undetectable without
a snapshot or witness.

## Export report (`report.html` / `report.md`)

`opencode-teamwork export` writes a human-readable report of one run. It is a
reporting output only: it is read by no engine tool, no agent, and no gate, and
deleting it changes nothing about the run.

**Where it is written.** Without `-o`, the file goes to the run directory:

- HTML (default): `.opencode/teamwork/<session-id>/report.html`
- Markdown (`-m` / `--markdown`): `.opencode/teamwork/<session-id>/report.md`

The CLI prints the **absolute** path of the file it wrote. With `-o <file>` the
report goes to that path instead. With `-o -` it is streamed to stdout and no file
is written. The export reads the run directory and never modifies it.

**Format: HTML.** A standalone single-file document. CSS is embedded in a `<style>`
block, and the file has no external CDN, fonts, scripts, or images. It works fully
offline and is safe to attach to an issue or archive. Dynamic text is HTML-escaped,
and absolute `http(s)://` URLs in quoted text are defanged, so the file contains no
live links.

**Format: Markdown.** GitHub-flavored Markdown with tables and a checklist. It is
suitable for pasting into a PR description or an issue comment.

**Contents** (both formats, in this order):

| Section | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Summary | `plan.dag.json`, `state.json`, `costs.json`, `events.jsonl`: session id, topology, overall status, phase, duration, budget, spend, tokens, task totals |
| Run terms | integrity mode, input-preflight status, final-verdict provenance, `victory` label, handoff-gate status, and artifact-authenticity display (envelope presence only; HMACs are not verified) |
| Tasks | one row per task: status, worker, verifier, rounds, duration, cost, checks. Details: summary, feedback, fatal findings, branch, worktree |
| Acceptance checklist | (Markdown) one box per task, ticked when `verified_pass`, plus the security gate |
| Security audit | `verify/security-audit.json`: pre-merge status, severity counts, findings |
| Final verification | `verify/final.json`, when present |
| Pitfalls | `pitfalls.md` entries |
| Other cost buckets | cost buckets that are not task ids (HTML only, when present) |
| Warnings | files that were oversize, unreadable, or malformed and were skipped |

**Run terms labels.** `victory` is copied from `verify/final.json` (for example
`CONFIRMED`, or `SKIPPED (explicit): <reason>`). The handoff gate is shown as
`required (PASS|MISSING|STALE|INVALID)` or `SKIPPED (explicit)`. Artifact
authenticity is **envelope presence only**: `signed` means an `_auth` object is
present (the export has no key and cannot verify the MAC), `unsigned` means it
is absent, and `unknown` means there is no final verdict. A final report that
reports `PASS` while required handoffs are unmet is marked
**ENGINE WOULD REJECT**; the export never upgrades that to a clean PASS claim.

The overall status is decided from three inputs: the tasks, the security audit, and
`verify/final.json`. It is checked in this order:

1. `FAIL` when any task is `verified_fail` or `blocked`, when the security audit
   reports `FAIL` or has any `critical` or `high` finding, or when
   `verify/final.json` reports `FAIL`.
2. `PASS` when `verify/final.json` reports `PASS` (even if some tasks are not yet
   `verified_pass`).
3. `PASS` when there is at least one task, every task is `verified_pass`, and the
   audit did not fail.
4. Otherwise `INCOMPLETE`. (If `tournament/` is present with phase `CANCELLED`, `BUDGET_HALTED`, or any non-`COMPLETED` phase, `export` never promotes the run to `PASS` via task fallback and reports `FAIL` or `INCOMPLETE`.)

Missing `events.jsonl` data is shown
as "timing unknown" rather than guessed.

**Errors.** A missing or invalid run (no run directory, or no valid
`plan.dag.json` / `state.json`) makes `export` exit with code `1`, as does a
file-write error.

# Guardrails

The security model for `@heretek-ai/opencode-teamwork-v2`, and how each control is enforced
(in code, not just in a prompt).

## Threat model

An agent that can **read untrusted content** (repo files, `prompt_draft.md`,
`state.json`, web pages, issues) and also **run shell / edit / fetch** is one
indirect-prompt-injection away from exfiltration or destruction. Teamwork agents
run with the user's full privileges by default, so the controls below exist to
remove the sharpest edges.

**Filesystem contract.** The claim, lock and containment guarantees hold **only
among processes on one host with a coherent filesystem**. Across hosts the
controls are best-effort duplicate suppression, **never exactly-once**; a
missing `host` is read as cross-host, so an incomplete record fails closed
rather than being treated as local.

## Known gaps / non-goals

- **No worktree/cwd confinement in code.** Worker/verifier prompts *say* "don't
  edit outside your worktree," but with `resource: "*"` nothing enforces it.
  `git worktree` isolation is prompt-level. (Mitigated only by the permission
  hook: for the verifier, scout, security auditor, and victory auditor it denies
  `edit` but not `shell`, which can write anywhere; the falsifier, segment
  reviewer, formalization reviewer, and referee also have `shell` denied.)
- **`constraints.network` is enforced for `webfetch` only.** When a run's
  `prompt_draft.md` or any per-task `spec.json` says `network: denied`, the
  permission hook denies `webfetch` for every `team/*` agent. `constraints.sandbox`
  remains descriptive, and `shell` can still reach the network: there is no
  sandbox for shell.
- **Plugin tool scoping is role-based, not capability isolation.** Every
  run-mutating `teamwork_*` tool checks the trusted session agent against
  `authorize.ts` and (for run-bound tools) descent from the plan-time
  `rootSessionId`. Read-only `status`/`resume`/`cost` remain available to every
  installed `team/*` role. This stops an arbitrary agent from calling
  `teamwork_security_audit`, `teamwork_final_verify`, `teamwork_victory_audit`,
  etc., but it is not an OS sandbox: a same-UID process outside the plugin can
  still write run files, and the artifact-trust boundary below still applies.
- **Victory-auditor independence is a fresh session, not capability
  isolation.** `team/victory-auditor` keeps `shell` (which can modify files) and
  is denied `edit`, `webfetch`, and `subagent`. Its independence comes from
  running in a fresh session that inspects the delivered artifacts and executes
  tests itself, not from a reduced capability set. There is no scoped
  test-runner tool; if one is added it must be role-scoped in `authorize.ts`
  and covered by the engine suite.
- **The SSRF guard covers plugin URL ingress, not shell.** `document.url` and
  preflight URL checks use `url-guard.ts`; an agent with `shell` or `webfetch`
  can still reach the network directly. `constraints.network: denied` remains a
  `webfetch`-only guard (see above).
- **Artifact authenticity is tamper-evident, not local-user-proof.**
  Control-plane artifacts carry an HMAC `_auth` envelope and a digest-index
  entry outside the run dir ([ADR 0005](adr/0005-artifact-authenticity.md)), so
  a run-dir-only writer can no longer forge a PASS, copy an envelope between
  files/runs, or downgrade the signed plan baseline. **This does not stop a
  same-UID shell:** with read access to `opencode.db` (or the plugin KV backing
  store) it can read the HMAC key and mint a valid envelope, and `ctx.storage`
  is in the same user account, so the digest index is not a separate privilege
  domain either. Moving the key to a
  same-UID helper, using the OS keychain, or gating on `ctx.permission.assert`
  does not fix this: a same-UID helper is a signing oracle, the keychain is
  same-UID accessible, and `assert` is auto-approvable under `--auto`. **No
  in-process, zero-dependency control fixes this.** Phase B options and the
  administrator-only requirements (separate UID/system service, TPM/`tss`
  access, SELinux labels) are assessed in
  [ADR 0006](adr/0006-artifact-trust-isolation.md), which recommends accepting
  and documenting this boundary for now; a real Phase B needs a different
  privilege domain and a non-oracle signing decision (a human-presence gate or
  an independent verifier). Until then, do not claim protection against a local
  user who can read the database, and do not describe artifacts as
  tamper-proof, signed by a trusted authority, or safe against a local user.
  Ed25519 (ADR 0008) makes it possible to *verify* with only a public key and
  adds declared trust levels, but a local private key or same-UID command
  signer is still readable/callable by that user; `SECURITY.md` carries the
  decision tree for the hardened profile. **Approval is not review:** 0.11.0
  requires a distinct Ed25519 approver key and an approval directory owned by
  another UID, and binds the approval to the **exact bytes of
  `prompt_draft.md`**, the run id, and a one-use nonce consumed under the plan
  lock. The signed manifest (version 3) records `specHash`/`specBytes`/
  `approvalDigest`/`approvalNonce`/`approvalBinding`/`approvedBy`/`approvedAt`,
  so an edited draft, another run's approval, or a replayed nonce is
  `AUTH_APPROVAL_STALE`/`_INCOMPLETE`/`_REPLAY` rather than accepted. The
  plugin signer and command signer refuse an `approvals/` path
  (`AUTH_APPROVAL_SCOPE`); only the approver key holder can produce one. It
  still treats `approvedBy`/`attestedBy` as a claimed `uid:`/`oidc:`/`ci:`
  label, not an identity proof, and does not establish that a human read the
  draft, that the displayed text matched the bytes hashed, or that the approval
  body is accurate. A single-UID host cannot satisfy the different-owner
  requirement at all, and the CLI's typed confirmation is not human-presence
  enforcement. The administrator-only deployment steps (separate signer UID,
  root-owned signer, socket service, audit rules, SELinux labels, verification)
  are in [ADMIN-HARDENING.md](ADMIN-HARDENING.md); the v2 signer contract is in
  [SIGNER-PROTOCOL.md](SIGNER-PROTOCOL.md). They are not in-process controls
  and are not enforced by the plugin. **0.14.0 witness and signer v2:** a
  witness receipt is `verified` only when `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_WITNESS_PUBLIC_KEY`
  is configured and the receipt signature covers the run, path, digest, nonce
  and signed time; otherwise it is `unverified` and detection-only. A forged KV
  receipt is `AUTH_INVALID`, not a pass. When
  `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER_APPROVAL_DIR` is set the plugin sends a v2 request
  with the derived `approvalRef`, but it does not read the approval: the
  signer's policy remains outside the plugin, and the signer is not shipped in
  this repository (see [ADR 0014](adr/0014-verifiable-witness-and-signer-v2.md)).
  Free-form inputs that are not control-plane verdicts (`state.json` task
  summaries, `pitfalls.md`, `prompt_draft.md`, spec text) remain untrusted and
  are sanitised before injection, not authenticated. **Handoff prose is in the
  same category:** the index entry is HMAC-signed on a signed plan, but the
  narrative itself is not a control-plane verdict, and a signature only proves
  which trusted session recorded which bytes — not that the sender actually
  observed what it wrote. Never treat a handoff as a PASS. The continuity gate
  can reject a run when a required handoff is missing, stale, unsigned on a
  `handoffAuth: "signed"` run, or its `_auth` does not verify (edited metadata,
  copied envelope, unknown key, missing index record). It still treats handoffs
  only as continuity evidence, never as a second verdict authority; the verdict
  still comes from reports, waves, and the victory audit.
  Per-agent briefings are a context convenience only: they duplicate shared
  briefing data plus agent identity, and an unreadable/refused per-agent copy
  falls back to the shared briefing (`agents/` is not a trust boundary).
- **Claim fencing is cooperative, not a lock service.** The fence and lease stop
  the engine from silent re-dispatch; they cannot stop a same-UID process (or a
  worker shell) from writing files after its claim was released. Fingerprints are
  a point-in-time heuristic: a change that is reverted exactly, a build artifact
  outside the scoped paths, or an untracked scan that exceeds 1000 files / 8 MiB
  (`unknown`) can be missed. `adopt`/`requeue` never commit, and manual
  `teamwork_cost` `addUsd` remains non-idempotent. There is no portable
  compare-and-swap on NFS, so exactly-once dispatch cannot be guaranteed there.
- **No sandbox for shell.** Agents run with full user privileges and network.
- **Read containment is platform-specific.** `safe-fs.mjs` enforces the
  post-open containment check only on Linux with a mounted, usable
  `/proc/self/fd`. If Linux procfs is unavailable, existing-file reads are
  refused (fail closed); absent files still read as absent. macOS and Windows
  have no pure-JS fd-to-path primitive, so they keep `O_NOFOLLOW`/lstat,
  `O_NONBLOCK`, `fstat` and the byte cap, and the intermediate-component symlink
  race remains a documented residual risk there.
- **Write containment is preventive on Linux, detective on macOS/Windows
  (ADR 0010/0013).** On Linux with a usable `/proc/self/fd`, run writers pin the
  parent directory and cannot be redirected by an intermediate swap. **Linux
  without procfs fails closed** (nothing is written). **macOS and Windows are
  detective**: there is no pure-JS dir-relative write without a native addon, so
  writers keep the path-based atomic write plus checks. 0.13.0 records the run
  root and every existing ancestor `(dev, ino)` at target time, re-stats them
  immediately before the create/rename/unlink and again in the post-check, and
  refuses a mismatch as `identity-changed` (a legitimately renamed run root
  fails closed). Each run also records its root identity in the signed manifest
  and re-checks it before control-plane writes. The first `mkdir` of a run root
  is still path-based. **A detected write is a report about an event that
  already happened, not a prevented one:** a transient swap that is reverted
  before the check can be missed, and a detected write is not rolled back.
  `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_REQUIRE_PINNED_WRITES=1` (or a plan's
  `requirePinnedWrites: true`) refuses control-plane writes on a non-pinned host
  with a named `containment-mode` refusal; default off. A same-UID process that
  can ptrace the plugin can observe or alter its descriptors. Containment stops
  redirection, not content forgery inside the run. **The guarantee is
  single-host:** a coherent local filesystem is assumed, a transient swap that
  is reverted before the detective check can still be missed, and a detected
  write is not rolled back. The durable anomaly audit is evidence for an
  operator; acknowledging an anomaly does not repair a refused artifact.

## Running an audit

Use the `team/security-auditor` agent (clean context; `edit` denied, `shell`
available) or a fresh subagent. It is also wired into the prompt linter's
expectations; the guardrail invariants (session-id validation present, no stale
references) are checked in CI by `scripts/lint-prompts.mjs`.

### 2.1 Storage is a global KV, not a per-session store

OBSERVED:

- The host exposes only `get`, `set`, `remove`, `scan` (`packages/plugin/src/promise/storage.ts:4-9`).
- Values are `Schema.Json`; the SQLite column is `text({ mode: "json" })`
  (`packages/core/src/kv.ts:9`, `packages/core/src/kv/sql.ts:5-9`).
- The plugin's key namespace is derived solely from the plugin id:
  `plugin:<hex-of-id>:`, so every session, location and worktree on that host
  shares one keyspace (`packages/core/src/plugin/host.ts:681-708`).
- `set` is an unconditional upsert (`onConflictDoUpdate`) with no
  compare-and-swap, no version, no lease and no expiry
  (`packages/core/src/kv.ts:49-56`); the table has only key/value/timestamps
  (`packages/core/src/kv/sql.ts:5-9`).

Consequences (INFERRED from the above):

- Two concurrent writers to the same key are last-writer-wins. Our run locks
  (`plugins/opencode-teamwork/locks.ts`) are therefore required for control
  plane writes; the KV must not be treated as a mutex.
- There is no TTL, so every index we keep must carry its own timestamp and be
  bounded/compacted by us.
- Nothing is scoped to a session, directory or workspace. A key that embeds a
  session id is the only isolation available.
- Values round-trip through JSON, so `undefined`, `NaN`, `BigInt`, functions and
  cycles are not representable.

- `<namespace with dots → underscores>_<normalized name>` when it is present.

The underscore form is what `editor.add` commits (`packages/core/src/tool.ts:
266-269`) and what a model calls as a direct tool. The dot form is what Code
Mode uses for `options.namespace` (below).

### 3.2 `editor.namespace` is catalog-only

OBSERVED:

- `editor.namespace({ name, description })` writes into `editor.namespaces`
  (`packages/core/src/tool.ts:258-265`). It has no effect on `add`, `update` or
  `effectiveName`.
- `add` derives the id from the **tool's own** `options.namespace`
  (`packages/core/src/tool.ts:266-269`).
- The only consumer of `namespaces` is the Code Mode inventory
  (`packages/core/src/tool.ts:346-349`), where it supplies a description for a
  path; tools are still placed by `qualifiedName(registration)`
  (`packages/core/src/codemode/tool.ts:503-514`, `:408-417`).

INFERRED: `editor.namespace("teamwork")` alone does **not** produce
`teamwork_plan`. It creates a namespace node that has no tools unless the added
tools declare `options.namespace: "teamwork"`. This is the root cause of the
bare-name defect in §4 row 1.

### 3.3 Code Mode is the default, and it hides direct tools

OBSERVED:

- `defaultCodeMode(tool) = tool.options?.codemode !== false`
  (`packages/core/src/tool/runtime.ts:307`).
- In `snapshot`, a tool is moved into the Code Mode inventory when Code Mode is
  available and `defaultCodeMode(tool)` is true; only tools with
  `codemode: false`, or explicitly kept direct, stay as direct tools
  (`packages/core/src/tool.ts:321-333`).
- Without Code Mode the same tools become direct, because otherwise they would
  be unreachable (`packages/core/src/tool.ts:312-314`).
- Inside Code Mode the callable path is the dot-qualified name
  (`packages/core/src/codemode/tool.ts:408-417`); the dispatcher accepts either
  the map key or the qualified name (`:503-514`).

INFERRED: a plugin that adds tools without `options.codemode: false` is
invisible as a direct tool on a Code Mode host. The model can still reach it
only by writing an `execute` program that calls the dot path. Prompts that say
"call `teamwork_plan`" do not match either form unless the namespace is declared.

### 3.4 Only `content` (and a declared `output`) reaches the model

OBSERVED (`packages/core/src/tool/runtime.ts:58-73`):

- With no output schema, the host returns `{ output: undefined, content:
  normalizeContent(result.content), metadata? }`. Any other key on the result
  object is dropped.
- With an output schema, `result.output` is encoded/validated and passed as
  `output`; `content` is normalized with the output as a fallback when content
  is empty.

INFERRED: returning `{ content, conflict: true, conflictingFiles }` does not
surface `conflict` or `conflictingFiles` to the model. Only the text in
`content` is visible (plus `metadata` if the caller inspects it). Extra keys are
dead weight, and a prompt that depends on them is depending on nothing.

### 3.5 An `output` key without a schema is a defect

OBSERVED (`packages/core/src/tool/runtime.ts:58-61`):

```ts
if (outputSchema === undefined) {
  if ("output" in result) return yield* Effect.die("Tool result declared output without an output schema")
  ...
}
```

`Effect.die` is a defect, not a typed `Tool.Error`. The call does not become a
normal tool failure with a message the model can act on; it escapes the
declared error channel. OBSERVED and load-bearing for §4 row 3.

Conversely, when an output schema **is** declared, a result without `output`
fails with `Tool.Error("Tool did not return its declared output")`
(`packages/core/src/tool/runtime.ts:67`).

### 3.6 A failed JSON-Schema conversion silently disables validation

OBSERVED:

- `codecFor` builds a codec inside `Result.try(...).pipe(Result.getOrUndefined)`
  and caches `undefined` on failure (`packages/core/src/tool/runtime.ts:15-20`).
- `validateInput` then does `if (codec === undefined) return { value }`
  (`packages/core/src/tool/runtime.ts:88-91`).

INFERRED: a malformed or unsupported JSON Schema on a tool input does not fail
registration. It makes that tool accept unvalidated input. The tool's own
`execute` body must therefore not assume the schema ran; our tools do their own
sanitisation, which is why this is a latent risk rather than an active exploit.

### 3.7 Excess input properties are stripped before the tool runs (closed plugin-side in 0.18.1)

OBSERVED:

- The runtime compiles a raw JSON-Schema input to an Effect codec and decodes
  with `onExcessProperty: "ignore"` (`packages/core/src/tool/runtime.ts:115-121`,
  `:187-201`).
- The built-in `opencode.tool.input.repair` plugin runs on `execute.before`
  (`packages/core/src/plugin/tool-input-repair.ts:32,41-58`). Its `repairObject`
  deletes every undeclared key when the schema says
  `additionalProperties: false` (`:161-171`), before the runtime validator sees
  the input.

INFERRED: `additionalProperties: false` alone does not reject an unknown key on
2.4.1; by the time any decoder runs, the repair pass has removed it. A tool
input that is a Standard Schema still receives this repaired object.

**Closed in 0.18.1 (ADR 0019).** Every Teamwork tool input is wrapped in
`strictInput()`, a Standard Schema. The runtime calls
`schema["~standard"].validate` and turns its `{path, message}` issues into
`Tool.Error` (`packages/core/src/tool/runtime.ts:76-82`, `:101-113`,
`:148-167`), while `jsonSchema.input` returns the original schema unchanged
(`:169-185`). The wrapper also attaches a non-enumerable empty
`patternProperties` to each closed object so the repair pass leaves unknown keys
in place; the validator then rejects them at the exact path. The catalog is
byte-identical, and L1 A4 plus L2 J1 assert the refusal. `additionalProperties:
true` records remain intentionally open.

`Tool.Result` is defined at `packages/schema/src/tool.ts:121-125`; `Tool.Info`
and `Options` at `:127-143`.

### 5.3 Assertions

Assert on **tool results and on-disk artifacts**, never on prompt prose or the
model's narration:

- tool return `content` and `metadata`, plus `output` only when a schema is
  declared;
- files under the run directory (bytes/digest, JSON shape);
- refusal codes (`AUTHZ_*`, `AUTH_*`, `STALE_FENCE`, …) and exit paths;
- host-visible catalog entries: effective id, namespace, whether the tool is
  direct or Code Mode only.

A test may assert that a prompt *contains* a tool name (a cheap regression for
the §4 row 1 defect), but it must not treat that as proof the tool exists. The
existence proof is the catalog, not the prompt.

### 5.4 The catalog golden is the first artifact

Capture, once, the result of `ctx.tool.list()` after every transform

- `id` (effective name),
- `options.namespace`,
- `options.codemode` and the resulting placement (`direct` or `codemode`),
- the input schema's `required` keys,
- a digest of the input/output JSON Schema.

Compare on every run. This is the one artifact that catches the bare-name and
Code Mode defects even before a model is involved, and its diff is readable in
review. It is also the artifact that would have caught the `2.3.2 → 2.4.1`

## 7. What no harness can prove

These remain residuals no matter how many layers pass. Each is a property of a
different principal or of the model, not of the plugin's code path.

| Residual | Why a harness cannot close it |
| --- | --- |
| **Prompt injection** | A scripted model follows a script. A live model reading an untrusted document is the attack, and a passing test only shows the injection used in the test did not work. |
| **Same-UID forgery** | The engine and the attacker share a UID in every test we can run. Reading the KV key ring and minting an envelope is not simulated by a test that uses the same key legitimately. |
| **Model judgment** | Whether `team/verifier` noticed the real defect is not a function of the harness; a passing scripted turn only proves the call was made. |
| **A consistent signed lie under `declared`** | Under `declared` provenance there is nothing to re-execute. A false PASS with a matching signature passes every check by construction; only `command` provenance plus external re-execution narrows it. |
| **NFS exactly-once** | Locks are `link`/`rename`-based and documented as best-effort off one local filesystem. A test on tmpfs cannot prove a network filesystem's semantics. |
| **Transient detective swaps** | The post-write `(dev, ino)` check can miss a symlink swapped and restored between syscalls. A test sees one interleaving. |
| **TUI rendering** | The harness drives the server API, not the terminal renderer. Layout, wrapping, colours and keybindings are outside it. |
| **Cost/quota truth** | The harness can assert what the host reports; it cannot prove a provider billed that amount. |

## 8. Version pinning decision

**Decision:** publish an **optional peer range** and warn at runtime; do not add
a runtime dependency.

- `package.json` gains:
  - `peerDependencies: { "@opencode/plugin": "^2.4.0" }`
  - `peerDependenciesMeta: { "@opencode/plugin": { "optional": true } }`
- `setup` compares `ctx.app.version` (`packages/core/src/app.ts:4-19`) against
  the audited major/minor and logs **one** warning on mismatch, including the
  `"unknown"` embedded-host case. It never refuses to load.
- Installs stay dependency-free: an optional peer is not installed by npm
  (INFERRED: npm optional-peer semantics; the current package manifest has no
  `dependencies` key at all — OBSERVED, `package.json`).
- The exact `@opencode/*@2.4.1` pins live only in the harness
  devDependencies, where reproducibility matters and consumers are unaffected.

Rationale (INFERRED): a hard `engines`-style refusal would break channel builds
and the embedded SDK, both of which legitimately report a different or unknown
version. A warning plus a tested range keeps the common case honest without
turning a minor drift into an outage. The peer range documents intent for
package managers and humans; the runtime warning covers hosts that never
resolve the peer.

# Signer protocol v2: from signing oracle to policy enforcement

**Status:** 0.14.0 implements the plugin half. The plugin sends `v: 2` with
`runId` and `approvalRef` when `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER_APPROVAL_DIR` is set,
and the exact v1 request when it is unset. This document specifies the contract
the signer must implement. The signer itself is **not in this repository** and
must be built (§8). A v2-only signer with an unmodified/0.13 client, or a v1-only
signer with the directory set, fails closed with `AUTH_SIGNER_UNAVAILABLE`; there
is no HMAC fallback. Do not deploy the two halves separately.

The runbook that installs the service, key directory and approvals is
[docs/ADMIN-HARDENING.md](ADMIN-HARDENING.md). The artifact envelope and digest
index are in [docs/adr/0005-artifact-authenticity.md](adr/0005-artifact-authenticity.md);
the signer SPI is in [docs/adr/0008-signer-spi-and-trust-levels.md](adr/0008-signer-spi-and-trust-levels.md).

> **The policy lives outside the plugin.** The plugin can verify that a
> signature matches a configured public key. It cannot verify that the signer
> checked an approval, that a human was present, or that a verdict is true. A
> malicious signer holding the key can sign anything; a user-writable plugin can
> be edited to skip its own checks. The signer's policy and the external
> verifier's trust in the signer key are the boundary.

---

## 1. Why v1 is an oracle

The v1 request is:

```json
{"v":1,"alg":"ed25519","keyId":"…","path":"…","digest":"…","nonce":"…","at":"…","message":"…"}
```

It contains no `runId` and no reference to an approval. A v1 signer has no
basis on which to distinguish:

- the plugin signing a verdict after its gate passed; and
- a same-UID shell asking for a signature over any `(path, digest)` it likes.

If the signer merely checks the algorithm, key id and schema and then signs, it
is a signing oracle. Moving the key to another UID or another socket does not
change that: the agent and the shell are the same principal. v2 adds the
missing decision input — a separate approval bound to the exact `runId`, path,
digest and nonce — and requires the signer to check it every time.

A signer that accepts v1 alongside v2 re-opens the oracle for any caller that
sends v1. A v2 signer must refuse `v: 1` with `E_VERSION`.

---

## 2. Request

One JSON object on stdin, one JSON object on stdout, no shell, bounded size
(256 KiB is a reasonable maximum). The process exits non-zero on refusal or
error. `message` is base64url of the exact UTF-8 signature input; the signer
must not sign the JSON wording of the request.

```json
{
  "v": 2,
  "op": "sign-artifact",
  "runId": "r-01J8Z5K8V6Q9W2M4N7P3S6T8X0",
  "alg": "ed25519",
  "keyId": "signer_test",
  "path": "verify/victory.json",
  "digest": "ebafa7996580c7e8623f2eb09c1e32ae1c3f8cef511dc1a8552c1a15313810da",
  "nonce": "AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA",
  "at": "2026-11-23T12:00:00.000Z",
  "approvalRef": "/var/lib/teamwork-approvals/signer/r-01J8Z5K8V6Q9W2M4N7P3S6T8X0/9f2c….json",
  "message": "dGVhbXdvcmstYXJ0aWZhY3QtdjEAZWQyNTUxOQBzaWduZXJfdGVzdAB2ZXJpZnkvdmljdG9yeS5qc29uAEFBQUFBQUFBQUFBQUFBQUFBQUFBQUEAeyJraW5kIjoidGVhbXdvcmsudGVzdCIsIm4iOjEsInZlcmRpY3QiOiJQQVNTIiwieiI6Imxhc3QifQ"
}
```

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `v` | Integer `2`. `1` or any other value is `E_VERSION`. |
| `op` | Exactly `"sign-artifact"`. Any other value is `E_OP`. |
| `runId` | The signed run id, matching `^[0-9A-Za-z][0-9A-Za-z._-]{0,63}$`. |
| `alg` | Exactly `"ed25519"`. |
| `keyId` | The signer's configured key id. The signer must not accept a caller-chosen key. |
| `path` | Run-relative artifact path: no leading `/`, no `..` segment, no empty segment, no NUL; not `approvals/` or `./approvals/` (`E_APPROVAL_SCOPE`). |
| `digest` | 64 lowercase hex characters; the keyed digest in §3. |
| `nonce` | The run nonce from the signed manifest; base64url, at least 16 decoded bytes. |
| `at` | ISO-8601 timestamp. **Not covered by the signature.** Use it only for a bounded clock-skew check; never as an authorization fact. |
| `approvalRef` | Absolute path to the signer approval in §4. Must resolve under the configured approval directory. |
| `message` | Base64url (no padding) of the exact signature input in §3. |

The request must be rejected if any field is missing, of the wrong type, or
outside its bound. Extra unknown fields are ignored only if the implementation
can prove they do not affect the signed message; rejecting them is safer.

---

## 3. The message and the digest

### 3.1 Signature input

The plugin builds this string and signs its UTF-8 bytes (the same construction
as ADR 0008):

```text
teamwork-artifact-v1\0ed25519\0<keyId>\0<path>\0<nonce>\0<canonicalJson(payload without _auth)>
```

- The separator is a single NUL byte (`0x00`).
- There are exactly **six** fields: domain, algorithm, key id, path, nonce,
  canonical JSON.
- `canonicalJson` is the plugin's canonical JSON: object keys sorted, no
  whitespace, JSON-string escaping. The artifact schema uses ASCII keys; a v2
  signer should reject a non-ASCII key to avoid a JS/Rust/Go sorting mismatch.
- A literal NUL cannot occur inside the canonical JSON: `JSON.stringify` and
  the canonicalizer escape it as `\u0000`. Splitting on NUL is therefore
  unambiguous.
- The plugin signs and verifies the **string**, not the base64url rendering.
  Decode `message`, validate UTF-8, and sign those bytes.

### 3.2 Keyed digest

`digest` is not a plain SHA-256 of the payload. It is the plugin's
`payloadDigest`:

```text
HMAC-SHA256(
  key     = ASCII bytes "teamwork-artifact-digest-v1",
  message = UTF-8 canonicalJson(payload without _auth)
)
```

encoded as 64 lowercase hex characters. The label is a public domain-separation
value, not a secret. The signer must recompute this from the canonical JSON
field in the message, then compare the recomputed value in constant time with
the request's `digest`. Separately, it must require the re-canonicalised JSON to
be byte-identical to field 6; that catches non-canonical input before the digest
comparison. The signer must not trust the request's `digest` without
recomputation.

### 3.3 Test vector

This vector is generated from `plugins/opencode-teamwork/approval-format.mjs`.
It is a test vector, not a production artifact.

Payload (without `_auth`):

```json
{"kind":"teamwork.test","n":1,"verdict":"PASS","z":"last"}
```

`path = "verify/victory.json"`, `nonce = "AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA"`,
`keyId = "signer_test"`.


## 4. The approval artifact

A signer approval is a separate Ed25519 artifact, owned by a principal other
than the workload, stored under the configured approval directory. It is not the
same artifact as the prompt approval used by `human-approved`/`ci-attested`
(ADR 0011), though it may use the same approver key.

### 4.1 Location and ownership

- `approvalRef` is absolute and must resolve under the signer's configured
  approval directory (for example `/var/lib/teamwork-approvals/signer/`).
- The layout is **one file per `(runId, path)`**:
  `<APPROVAL_DIR>/<runId>/<sha256(path)>.json`, where `sha256(path)` is the plain
  (unkeyed) SHA-256 of the UTF-8 run-relative path, hex-encoded. The plugin
  derives it with `contentSha256Hex` in
  `plugins/opencode-teamwork/approval-format.mjs`; the producer
  (`opencode-teamwork approve signer`) writes the same path. This is deliberately
  **not** the keyed artifact digest (`payloadDigest`/`sha256Hex`).
- The directory and file must be owned by the configured approver UID (or, at
  minimum, not by the workload UID). The runbook uses a dedicated
  `teamwork-approver`.
- The file is a regular file, not a symlink, at most 64 KiB, mode `0640` with a
  group the signer can read. The workload must not be in that group or be able
  to write the directory.
- The filename is not a policy input: the signed payload binds the policy
  fields, and the signer must recompute the expected reference rather than trust
  a caller-chosen path. A copied file with the same fields is the same
  authorization for the same `(runId, path, digest, nonce)`.

### 4.2 Payload

```json
{
  "v": 1,
  "kind": "teamwork.signer-approval",
  "approvalId": "b7Q…base64url at least 16 bytes…",
  "runId": "r-01J8Z5K8V6Q9W2M4N7P3S6T8X0",
  "path": "verify/victory.json",
  "digest": "ebafa7996580c7e8623f2eb09c1e32ae1c3f8cef511dc1a8552c1a15313810da",
  "nonce": "AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA",
  "approvedAt": "2026-11-23T11:55:00.000Z",
  "expiresAt": "2026-11-24T11:55:00.000Z",
  "approvedBy": "uid:approver",
  "note": "optional text; not a policy input",
  "_auth": {
    "alg": "ed25519",
    "keyId": "approval_…",
    "sig": "base64url Ed25519 signature"
  }
}
```

`approvedBy` must match `uid:<name>`, `oidc:<issuer>#<sub>`, or
`ci:<workflow>`. It is a claimed label, not an identity proof. `note` is
optional and covered by the signature but is not used for authorization; do not
let free text change a decision.

In 0.14.0 the producer is
`opencode-teamwork approve signer --session <runId> --path <relPath> --digest
<64hex>`, which writes the file at the §4.1 layout. It sets `nonce` to the run
nonce read from the signed `run.manifest.json` (not a fresh random value, which
could not match the request) and carries no prompt-approval field.

### 4.3 Approval signature input

Use a distinct domain so an artifact signature can never be reused as an
approval (or the reverse):

```text
teamwork-signer-approval-v1\0<runId>\0<path>\0<digest>\0<nonce>\0<expiresAt>\0<canonicalJson(approval payload without _auth)>
```

The signature is Ed25519 over the UTF-8 bytes of that string, verified with the
configured approver public key. `_auth.keyId` must equal the configured
approver key id. The approval `_auth` is not an artifact envelope; it uses the
domain above, not the artifact domain. The `approvedAt` field is inside the
canonical payload and is therefore signed; `expiresAt` is both signed and
separately compared. An approval with an unknown `kind`, a missing field, an
HMAC `_auth`, a different domain, or a different approver key is
`E_APPROVAL_SIG` or `E_APPROVAL_BINDING`.

### 4.4 Replay and expiry

- `runId`, `path`, `digest` and `nonce` must equal the request exactly.
- `expiresAt` must be in the future at signing time; `approvedAt` must not be
  in the future beyond a small skew. The lifetime is bounded (24 hours by
  default; 7 days maximum, matching the approval TTL policy).
- A replay of the **same** approval for the **same** `(runId, path, digest,
  nonce)` is idempotent: it authorizes the same artifact again. A replay for a
  different path or digest fails the binding check.
- If the deployment needs a strict single-use decision, the signer keeps a
  durable ledger keyed by `approvalId` (and a hash of the request) and refuses a
  different request that reuses it. That ledger is signer state; a crash must
  fail closed, not reset the ledger silently. Do not claim single-use without
  it.

## 5. The six checks the signer performs

Perform them in this order. Every failure returns a named error and no `sig`.
Do not sign first and check later.

### Check 1 — Version, operation, algorithm, key id, time

- `v === 2` (`E_VERSION`); `op === "sign-artifact"` (`E_OP`).
- `alg === "ed25519"` (`E_ALG`); `keyId === configured key id` (`E_KEYID`).
- `runId` matches the run-id pattern; `path` is a valid run-relative path and
  is not under `approvals/` (`E_PATH`, `E_APPROVAL_SCOPE`).
- `at` parses and is within the configured skew (`E_REQUEST`). Treat a clock
  failure as a refusal, not as "probably fine".

### Check 2 — Split and validate the message

- Strict base64url decode (no padding, no whitespace, canonical re-encode
  equality); reject invalid UTF-8 (`E_MESSAGE`).
- Split on NUL into exactly six fields (`E_MESSAGE`).
- Field 1 is exactly `teamwork-artifact-v1`; field 2 is `ed25519`; field 3 is
  the request `keyId`; field 4 is the request `path`; field 5 is the request
  `nonce` (`E_MESSAGE`).
- Parse field 6 as a JSON object. Reject arrays, scalars, duplicate keys,
  non-ASCII keys, and non-finite numbers (`E_CANONICAL`).
- Re-canonicalise the parsed payload and require byte equality with field 6
  (after UTF-8 encoding). This rejects reordered keys, whitespace, and
  alternate escapes (`E_CANONICAL`).

### Check 3 — Recompute the digest

- Compute the keyed digest in §3.2 over the canonical JSON.
- Compare it in constant time with `request.digest`; require 64 lowercase hex
  (`E_DIGEST`).
- The signature the signer returns is over the **message bytes**, not over the
  digest. The digest is the envelope field the plugin records; a mismatch means
  the request is internally inconsistent.

### Check 4 — Open the approval safely

- Require `approvalRef` to be absolute, with no `..` segment, under the
  configured approval directory. Resolve the directory once and keep a
  descriptor.
- Open the approval directory with `O_DIRECTORY|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC`, verify
  it is a directory owned by the configured approver (or at least not the
  workload), and keep that descriptor for the file open. When peer credentials
  are available (`SO_PEERCRED`), require the peer UID to be the configured
  workload UID; a different peer is `E_PEER`.
- Open the file relative to the directory descriptor with
  `O_RDONLY|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC` (`openat2` with
  `RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS|RESOLVE_BENEATH` if available). `O_NOFOLLOW` protects
  only the final component; the directory descriptor protects the parent.
- `fstat` the opened descriptor; require a regular file, size at most 64 KiB,
  and owner UID equal to the configured approver UID (or at minimum **not** the
  workload UID). Require no group/other write. Reject a file whose
  `(dev, ino, uid, mode)` changed between the pre-open check and `fstat`
  (`E_APPROVAL_OPEN`, `E_APPROVAL_OWNER`).
- Read the bounded bytes and parse JSON. Do not trust the filename or a
  caller-supplied digest to identify the file.

### Check 5 — Verify the approval signature and binding

- Require `v === 1` and `kind === "teamwork.signer-approval"`.
- `_auth.alg === "ed25519"`, `_auth.keyId === configured approver key id`, and
  the signature verifies over the §4.3 input with the approver public key
  (`E_APPROVAL_SIG`).
- Require `runId`, `path`, `digest`, `nonce` equal the request exactly
  (`E_APPROVAL_BINDING`). A mismatch on any one field is a refusal.
- Require `expiresAt` in the future, `approvedAt` not beyond the skew, and the
  lifetime within the configured maximum (`E_APPROVAL_EXPIRED`).
- Require `approvedBy` to match the `uid:`/`oidc:`/`ci:` shape, and
  `approvalId` to be present and at least 16 decoded bytes (`E_APPROVAL_BINDING`).
- If a durable `approvalId` ledger is enabled, check and update it atomically.
  A ledger write failure is a refusal (`E_APPROVAL_REPLAY`/`E_INTERNAL`).

### Check 6 — Append the audit line, then sign

- Append one line, before returning the signature, to a sink outside the
  workload's write domain. Include at least: `at`, `peerUid` (from
  `SO_PEERCRED` when available, otherwise the configured workload UID),
  `runId`, `path`, `digest`, `keyId`, `approvalId`, `approvalRef`, `decision`,
  and a hash of the request. Open the sink `O_APPEND|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC`,
  `fstat` it as a regular file, and `fsync` before signing.
- If the audit append fails, return `E_AUDIT` and **do not sign**. An
  unrecorded signature is a policy failure.
- Sign the decoded `message` bytes with Ed25519. Return exactly
  `{"alg":"ed25519","keyId":"<configured>","sig":"<base64url>"}` on stdout and
  exit 0.
- Never log the message or payload at a level that stores artifact content;
  log path, run id, digest and decision only. Error messages must not include
  key material or a partial signature.

## 6. Response and failure vocabulary

Success:

```json
{"alg":"ed25519","keyId":"signer_2f9c…","sig":"base64url 64-byte Ed25519 signature"}
```

Failure (stdout; exit non-zero; no `sig`):

```json
{"ok":false,"code":"E_APPROVAL_BINDING","message":"approval path does not match request"}
```

| Code | Meaning | Retry? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `E_VERSION` | `v` is not 2 (including v1) | No; fix the caller. |
| `E_OP` | Unsupported `op` | No. |
| `E_ALG` | Not `ed25519` | No. |
| `E_KEYID` | Wrong key id | No. |
| `E_REQUEST` | Missing/wrong-type field, bad runId/path, bad time | No. |
| `E_MESSAGE` | Bad base64url/UTF-8/NUL split/field mismatch | No. |
| `E_CANONICAL` | Non-canonical JSON, duplicate/non-ASCII key, bad number | No. |
| `E_PATH` | Path traversal, absolute path, empty segment | No. |
| `E_NONCE` | Missing/weak/mismatched nonce | No. |
| `E_DIGEST` | Recomputed digest does not match `digest` | No. |
| `E_APPROVAL_REF` | `approvalRef` absent, not absolute, outside the approval dir | No. |
| `E_APPROVAL_OPEN` | Symlink, non-regular, too large, changed identity | No. |
| `E_APPROVAL_OWNER` | Wrong owner (workload or unexpected principal) | No. |
| `E_APPROVAL_SIG` | Bad/missing approval signature or key id | No. |
| `E_APPROVAL_BINDING` | `runId`/`path`/`digest`/`nonce`/`approvedBy` mismatch | No. |
| `E_APPROVAL_EXPIRED` | Expired, not yet valid, or overlong lifetime | No. |
| `E_APPROVAL_REPLAY` | Reused approval id for a different request | No. |
| `E_APPROVAL_SCOPE` | Attempt to sign an `approvals/` path | No; the approval CLI owns that path. |
| `E_PEER` | Socket peer UID is not the configured workload UID | No; root is outside the policy. |
| `E_AUDIT` | Audit append failed | No; signing is refused. |
| `E_INTERNAL` | Unexpected internal error | Maybe; fail closed, never fall back. |

### 6.1 Plugin-side fail-closed mapping

The plugin's `spawnJson` verifies the response shape and signature. Any of the
following is `AUTH_SIGNER_UNAVAILABLE` and the write fails; there is no
fallback to the local HMAC key:

- a non-zero exit, a timeout, a malformed/partial response, or stderr noise;
- a response without `alg === "ed25519"`, the expected `keyId`, or a 64-byte
  `sig`;
- a signature that does not verify with `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER_PUBLIC_KEY`;
- a response containing `{"ok":false,...}` (it is not a signature response).

A future plugin may surface the signer's `code` as a named
`AUTH_SIGNER_REFUSED` or `AUTH_APPROVAL_*` error, but it must remain
fail-closed. Do not add an automatic retry with a different digest, a local
key, or a lower trust level. A transport retry with the **identical** request
is acceptable only if the signer is idempotent for the same approval; a
different request is a new policy decision.

## 7. Plugin side (implemented in 0.14.0)

0.14.0 makes exactly this change; the list remains the contract a replacement
plugin must satisfy:

1. **Send `v: 2` and `op: "sign-artifact"`** from the command-signer adapter
   (`signerEnvelope` in `plugins/opencode-teamwork/auth.ts`) when
   `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER_APPROVAL_DIR` is set.
2. **Carry `runId`** through `signRunArtifact` → `signArtifact` (the optional
   `runId` on `SignOptions`). A v2 signer must refuse an artifact with no run id.
3. **Derive `approvalRef` from trusted state**, not from an agent tool argument:
   `approvalRef = <OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER_APPROVAL_DIR>/<runId>/<contentSha256Hex(path)>.json`.
   The run id is validated against `^[0-9A-Za-z][0-9A-Za-z._-]{0,63}$`; the path
   hash is the plain SHA-256 from `approval-format.mjs`. Do not accept a
   caller-supplied `approvalRef`; the agent must not choose which approval to
   present.
4. **Configure the approval directory** with
   `OPENCODE_TEAMWORK_SIGNER_APPROVAL_DIR` (present in 0.14.0). It must be
   absolute, an existing real directory, and owned by a principal other than
   the workload; a configured-but-unusable directory fails
   `AUTH_SIGNER_UNAVAILABLE` before any spawn. When it is unset, the plugin
   keeps the exact v1 request for compatibility.
5. **Do not verify the approval in the plugin.** The plugin cannot know whether
   the approver is a human or whether the signer applied its policy. It verifies
   the returned signature only. Duplicating the approval check in the plugin
   would create a second, weaker policy and a false sense of assurance.
6. **Keep the fail-closed path.** A configured but unavailable or refusing
   signer must never fall back to the local key. The existing
   `AUTH_SIGNER_UNAVAILABLE` behavior is correct.

**Compatibility matrix.**

| Plugin | Signer | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| dir set (v2) | v2 | v2 request; the signer decides. |
| dir unset (v1) | v1 | exact v1 request; the signer is only as good as its own policy. |
| dir set (v2) | v1-only | the signer refuses; `AUTH_SIGNER_UNAVAILABLE`, no fallback. |
| dir unset (v1) | v2-only | the signer refuses `E_VERSION`; `AUTH_SIGNER_UNAVAILABLE`, no fallback. |

**What the plugin still cannot do.** It can verify a signature; it cannot verify
a policy. A same-UID writer can edit the plugin to skip the signer entirely, or
change the public key it trusts. The external verifier must pin the signer
public key outside the workload's write domain. That is why the policy and the
key custody are deployment properties.

## 8. Reference implementation outline

### 8.1 Language and process model

Use **Rust or Go** for the key-holding service. Both can enforce
`MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes` and read `SO_PEERCRED` from the accepted Unix
socket. A Node implementation is possible with `node --jitless`, but core
`node:net` does not expose peer credentials (observed in the feasibility spike),
and a JIT is incompatible with `MemoryDenyWriteExecute`; use Node only if the
approval-owner check is by configured UID and the service actually starts under
the directive. Test the real binary.

One request per connection, one response, then exit (systemd `Accept=yes` with
`StandardInput=socket`/`StandardOutput=socket`). Bound the read (256 KiB) and
the wall clock. No shell, no network, no secret in argv or environment. Load the
key from a `0600` file owned by the signer UID; keep it in memory only as long
as needed and zero it where the language supports it.

### 8.2 Modules

| Module | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `config` | Key id, key path, approval dir, approver uid/key, workload uid, audit sink, skew/TTL bounds. |
| `protocol` | Strict request parsing, base64url, UTF-8, NUL split, response encoding. |
| `canonical` | Canonical JSON matching the plugin's `approval-format.mjs`; duplicate-key and non-ASCII-key rejection. |
| `digest` | HMAC-SHA256 with the `teamwork-artifact-digest-v1` label; constant-time compare. |
| `approval` | `openat`/`openat2` with `O_NOFOLLOW`, `fstat`, owner/mode checks, signature and binding checks. |
| `audit` | Append, `fstat`, `fsync`, failure-is-refusal. |
| `sign` | Ed25519 over the decoded message bytes; response shape. |

Rust crates: `ed25519-dalek`, `hmac`, `sha2`, `serde`/`serde_json` (or a small
canonical encoder), `rustix`/`nix` for `openat2`, `fstat`, `SO_PEERCRED`.
Go: `crypto/ed25519`, `crypto/hmac`, `crypto/sha256`, `encoding/json` plus a
custom canonical encoder, `golang.org/x/sys/unix`. Do not use a JSON encoder
that sorts differently or escapes non-ASCII differently from the plugin; test
the vector in §3.3 and add non-ASCII value cases.

### 8.3 Configuration example

```text
--key-id signer_2f9c…
--key-file /var/lib/teamwork-signer/keys/signer.pem
--approval-dir /var/lib/teamwork-approvals/signer
--approver-uid 996                 # teamwork-approver
--workload-uid 997                # opencode
--approver-key /etc/teamwork/approver-ed25519.pub
--audit-log /var/log/teamwork/signer-audit.jsonl
--max-request-bytes 262144
--max-approval-bytes 65536
--max-approval-ttl 24h
--clock-skew 300s
```

The audit log path must be root-owned or signer-owned and not writable by the
workload. A signer-owned log can be rewritten by a compromised signer; forward
it to a remote sink if the audit is evidence.

### 8.4 Unit-test list

Protocol and canonicalisation:

1. v1 refused (`E_VERSION`); v2 accepted.
2. Bad base64url, padding, whitespace, invalid UTF-8 (`E_MESSAGE`).
3. Wrong domain, wrong field count, NUL inside a field (`E_MESSAGE`).
4. Key order/whitespace differences rejected (`E_CANONICAL`).
5. Duplicate keys rejected; non-ASCII keys rejected; non-finite numbers
   rejected.
6. The §3.3 vector reproduces the exact digest and message.
7. Non-ASCII **values** round-trip; escaping matches the plugin.
8. Request larger than the bound is refused.

Policy:

9. `alg`, `keyId`, `op`, `runId` and `path` mismatches.
10. Absolute path, `..`, empty segment, and `approvals/` path (`E_PATH`,
    `E_APPROVAL_SCOPE`).
11. Digest mismatch (`E_DIGEST`); constant-time comparison.
12. Missing approval ref; ref outside the approval dir; ref with `..`.
13. Approval symlink, non-regular file, oversized file, changed identity.
14. Approval owned by the workload (`E_APPROVAL_OWNER`).
15. Bad approval signature; wrong approver key id; HMAC approval.
16. Each binding field mismatch: `runId`, `path`, `digest`, `nonce`.
17. Expired, not-yet-valid, overlong lifetime; clock skew.
18. Reused `approvalId` for a different request (ledger enabled).
19. A failed audit append returns `E_AUDIT` and no signature.
20. A valid request returns a signature that verifies over the decoded message
    bytes with the public key.

Service and integration:

21. Peer UID mismatch (when `SO_PEERCRED` is used).
22. Partial/oversized/timeout reads; process exits without a signature.
23. Key file unreadable/wrong mode; startup fails closed.
24. Plugin sends v2 with `runId`/`approvalRef`; happy path writes `_auth`.
25. Plugin with signer stopped: `AUTH_SIGNER_UNAVAILABLE`; no HMAC fallback.
26. v2-only signer + an unmodified/v1 client (directory unset): every request
    refused; the failure is visible and does not silently downgrade.
27. External verifier accepts only the signer public key; a local HMAC
    envelope fails the trust level.
28. Key rotation: old artifacts verify with the old public key; new requests
    use the new key id; the private key never appears in logs or responses.

## 9. Do not ship a bare oracle signer

The following are all signing oracles, regardless of the key's location:

- a signer that accepts `v: 1` and signs any well-formed request;
- a signer that checks the schema, key id and path allowlist but does not check
  an approval or independently recompute the verdict;
- a signer that trusts `request.digest` without recomputing it from the
  message;
- a signer that accepts any `approvalRef` without verifying its owner,
  signature and binding;
- a signer that signs before appending the audit line, or ignores an audit
  failure;
- a signer that runs as the workload UID, or reads its key from an environment
  variable the workload can read;
- a signer that falls back to a local key, a cached signature, or a lower trust
  level when the policy fails;
- a signer that accepts a caller-chosen `approvalRef` from an agent tool.

A different UID, a socket mode or a root-owned binary is not enough by itself.
The policy is what makes the signer non-oracle.

---

## 10. Honest limits

- **Same-UID reachability.** The socket is reachable by the workload UID, and
  any same-UID process can call it. `SO_PEERCRED` names a UID, not a process or
  a user intent; the agent and a shell are the same principal. The approval
  binding is the only thing that distinguishes a permitted signing operation
  from an arbitrary one.
- **Human presence and key custody are deployment properties.** The signer can
  verify that a configured approver key signed the exact fields. It cannot
  establish that a human was present, that a human read the draft, that the
  displayed text matched the bytes hashed, or that the approver understood the
  consequence. `approvedBy` is a claimed label; a script with the approver key
  can reproduce the CLI's typed confirmation.
- **Approval content is not validated.** The signer does not know whether the
  approved verdict is true. An independent verifier that recomputes from
  evidence is a different design; it must define which evidence it trusts.
- **Compromise.** A compromised signer, signer key, approver key or host
  defeats the policy. Root can read the key, ptrace the service, edit the unit
  and rewrite the audit log.
- **Audit.** The audit line is a record, not proof. A local log can be erased by
  root or a compromised signer; forward it if it is evidence.
- **Clock and replay.** `expiresAt` is signed; `at` is not. Clock skew can
  reject a valid request or accept one outside the intended window. A replay of
  the same approval for the same artifact is idempotent; strict single-use needs
  a durable ledger.
- **Run id binding.** The artifact signature input does not contain `runId`; the
  run id is bound by the approval and by the per-run nonce pinned in the signed
  manifest. Do not claim that the artifact signature alone names the run. If a
  deployment needs `runId` inside the signature domain, define a new artifact
  domain version rather than changing v2 silently.
- **Plugin tampering.** The plugin is user-owned. A same-UID writer can disable
  its local gate or change the public key it trusts. The external verifier's
  pin and the signer's refusal are the remaining controls.
- **Availability.** A stopped signer fails every signed write closed. That is
  the intended behavior, but it is an availability dependency; plan a restart

  mismatch directions fail closed (`AUTH_SIGNER_UNAVAILABLE`). Do not describe a
